## Learning goals

This chapter is about measurement: how economists turn millions of transactions into a few
numbers that describe a whole economy. By the end of it you will be able to:

- derive why **production = expenditure = income**: value added adds up to final sales, and the
  national income identity $Y = C + I + G + NX$ splits GDP by who buys it;
- describe how the composition of U.S. GDP and **labor's share** of income have changed since 1929,
  and derive the labor-share measure that splits proprietors' income;
- derive the **Laspeyres**, **Paasche** and **chain-weighted** growth rates of real GDP as weighted
  averages, and split nominal growth into **inflation** and real growth;
- compare GDP across countries with exchange rates and **purchasing power parity**, and read the
  comparative statics of each conversion;
- read CSV files with pandas, compute new columns, work with dates, and draw area and line charts
  with Plotly Express;
- compare countries, and check that two data sources use the same definitions before you compare them.

<!-- cell -->

## Model overview

Back on **Islandia**, the island country we met in Chapter 1, a small statistics office has a job to do every year: put one number on everything the island produced. Farms grow grain, mills grind it, bakeries sell bread, Harbor Boatworks builds boats, the Islandia Treasury hires teachers, and some goods arrive by ship from Mainland. How do the statisticians add all of that up without counting anything twice? How do they tell a richer year from a year in which only prices went up? And how can Islandia compare itself with Mainland, which pays in another currency? This section builds the accounting tools that answer these three questions, following Islandia's statisticians step by step.

::: {.callout-note .mo-bigidea title="The big idea"}
**The question.** How do we turn millions of purchases and paychecks into a few numbers that describe a whole economy, and compare them across years and across countries?

**The answer in one sentence.** **Gross domestic product** (GDP), the market value of all final goods and services produced in a period, gives the same total whether we add up production, spending or income, and dividing it by the right price level turns it into real output that can be compared over time and between countries.

**What goes in and what comes out.** This chapter has no behavior to model and no parameters to choose. In go data: prices and quantities, producers' sales and purchases, incomes, exchange rates and price levels. Out come is GDP and its shares, labor's share of income, real GDP, the price level and inflation, and GDP at common prices.

**Road map.**

1. [Production, expenditure and income](#production-expenditure-and-income): why the three ways of counting GDP agree, the [national income identity](#deriving-the-results) and labor's share.
2. [Real GDP: quantity indexes and chain weighting](#real-gdp-quantity-indexes-and-chain-weighting): how to strip out price changes with the Laspeyres, Paasche and chained indexes.
3. [Price indexes and inflation](#price-indexes-and-inflation): how nominal growth splits into inflation and real growth.
4. [Comparing countries: exchange rates and purchasing power parity](#comparing-countries-exchange-rates-and-purchasing-power-parity): how to compare economies that use different currencies.
5. [Model in code](#model-in-code): the formulas as Python functions, checked with numbers, including Islandia's apples and computers (Table 2.4).

**Notation.** A bar over a letter marks a **parameter**, a number we choose; this chapter has none. Every letter below is a variable measured in the data, which later chapters call **endogenous** once a model explains it. All the results of this section are **identities**: they hold in any data set because of the way the variables are defined, which makes them useful checks on the data.

| Symbol | Meaning | Type |
|---|---|---|
| $R_j, M_j, VA_j$ | revenue, purchased intermediate inputs and value added of producer $j$ | endogenous |
| $Y$ | GDP | endogenous |
| $C, I, G$ | consumption, investment and government purchases | endogenous |
| $X, IM, NX$ | exports, imports and net exports $X - IM$ | endogenous |
| $p_{i,t}, q_{i,t}$ | price and quantity of good $i$ in year $t$ | endogenous |
| $s_{i,t}$ | share of good $i$ in spending in year $t$ | endogenous |
| $P_t$ | price level of the whole economy (the GDP deflator) | endogenous |
| $\pi$ | inflation rate, the growth rate of $P_t$ | endogenous |
| $e$ | exchange rate: units of the home currency per dollar | endogenous |
| $t, i, j$ | year, good and producer | notation |
| $g$, $\Delta x$ | a growth rate, and the change in $x$ between two years | notation |
:::

### Production, expenditure and income

#### Definitions

- A **final good** ends up with its last user: a household, a firm that keeps it as capital, the government, or a buyer abroad. An **intermediate good** disappears into some other good made in the same period, like the grain in Islandia's bread or the electricity that runs a mill.
- Producer $j$ earns **revenue** $R_j$ from its sales and pays $M_j$ for the **intermediate inputs** it buys. The difference is its **value added**, the part of the value of its output that it created itself:
  $$VA_j \equiv R_j - M_j.$$
- **Capital** (buildings, machines, boats, software) helps to make output but is not used up within the period. Its wear and tear is called **depreciation**. GDP is *gross* because depreciation is not taken out; subtracting it gives net domestic product.
- Value added is paid out as **income**: compensation of employees (wages, salaries and benefits), taxes on production less subsidies, depreciation, and the **net operating surplus**, which goes to the owners. The operating surplus is whatever is left, so the four pieces always add up to value added.
- **Spending** on final goods comes in four parts: consumption $C$; investment $I$ (business structures, equipment, intellectual property products such as software and R&D, new housing, and the change in inventories); government purchases $G$; and net exports $NX$, exports $X$ minus imports $IM$. When the Islandia Treasury hires a teacher or buys a ferry, that is part of $G$. When it pays a pension, or interest on its debt, it only moves income from some islanders to others and buys nothing, so that payment is not part of $G$.
- Only **new production** counts. Selling a used boat a second time produces nothing new, but the dealer's margin does count: it pays for the service of finding a buyer.

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: value added adds up to final sales.** Picture a chain of $J$ producers. The first buys no inputs, each one sells all of its output to the next, and the last one sells to final users. So $M_1 = 0$ and $M_j = R_{j-1}$, and

$$VA_1 = R_1, \qquad VA_2 = R_2 - R_1, \qquad \dots, \qquad VA_J = R_J - R_{J-1}.$$

Now add them up. Each revenue except the last shows up twice: with a plus sign as the seller's revenue, and with a minus sign as the buyer's cost. So the sum *telescopes*:

$$\sum_{j=1}^{J} VA_j = R_1 + (R_2 - R_1) + \dots + (R_J - R_{J-1}) = R_J.$$

The same cancellation works in any web of sales between firms, because each sale of an intermediate good is revenue for one firm and a cost for another. Counting production and counting final sales therefore give the same GDP:

$$\text{GDP} = \sum_j VA_j = \text{value of the final goods and services}.$$

::: {.callout-tip .mo-inwords title="In words: count each stage once"}
If Islandia's statisticians simply added up every firm's sales, the grain inside a loaf of bread would be counted twice: once when the farm sells it to the mill, and again inside the price of the bread. Subtracting what each firm bought from other firms keeps only its own contribution, so every stage of the chain is counted exactly once.
:::

**Step 2: production = income.** Add up the income split of value added over all producers:

$$\text{GDP} = \text{compensation} + \text{taxes on production less subsidies} + \text{net operating surplus} + \text{depreciation}.$$

Since the operating surplus is the leftover, every dollar of value added ends up as somebody's income. In practice, though, statisticians measure income from other records (tax returns, payrolls) than the ones they use for spending. The income total is called **gross domestic income** (GDI), and the small gap between GDI and GDP is the *statistical discrepancy*.

**Step 3: production = expenditure.** Final goods are bought by households, firms, the government and foreigners. So buyers at home spend $C + I + G$, and buyers abroad spend $X$. Some of what $C$, $I$ and $G$ buy, though, was made abroad and is not domestic production. Taking those imports out leaves the domestic output that went to final users: $C + I + G + X - IM$. And goods that were made this year but not sold? They count as **inventory investment**, part of $I$, as if the producer had bought its own output. So every unit produced has a buyer somewhere in the accounts:

$$Y = C + I + G + NX, \qquad NX \equiv X - IM.$$

This is the **national income identity**: GDP $Y$ seen from the spending side.

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: GDP counted three ways"}
$$\text{GDP} = \sum_j VA_j = \text{value of the final goods and services} \tag{1}$$

$$Y = C + I + G + NX, \qquad NX \equiv X - IM \tag{2}$$

Equation (1): value added and final sales give the same total, which Step 2 shows is also paid out as income. Equation (2) splits it by buyer.

**Islandia in numbers.** An Islandia farm sells grain worth \$40 to a mill, the mill sells flour worth \$70 to a bakery, and the bakery sells bread worth \$120 to islanders. The value added is $40 + 30 + 50 = 120$, exactly the value of the bread. Adding up all sales would give $230$.
:::

**Step 4: shares of GDP.** Divide both sides of (2) by $Y$ ([Appendix C.2](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.2-percentages-ratios-and-index-numbers)):

$$1 = \frac{C}{Y} + \frac{I}{Y} + \frac{G}{Y} + \frac{NX}{Y}.$$

The four shares sum to 100 percent in every year. Now compare two years. The left side is 1 in both, so its change is zero:

$$\Delta\frac{C}{Y} + \Delta\frac{I}{Y} + \Delta\frac{G}{Y} + \Delta\frac{NX}{Y} = 0.$$

If one share goes up, others must come down (Fig. 2). We compute shares from *nominal* values; the second block explains why.

**Step 5: labor's share of income.** We want the part of income that pays for work. Two items belong neither clearly to labor nor clearly to capital. Taxes on production $T$ (such as sales taxes) are nobody's labor or capital income. **Proprietors' income** $\mathit{Prop}$, what the self-employed earn, pays both for their own work and for their own equipment, like an islander who fishes from a boat she owns. Income net of these taxes is

$$\text{GDI} - T = \text{compensation} + \mathit{Prop} + \text{other capital income}.$$

Assume that labor gets the same fraction of proprietors' income as it gets of all other income, and call that fraction $\theta$:

$$\theta = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - T - \mathit{Prop}}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \text{compensation} = \theta\,(\text{GDI} - T - \mathit{Prop}).$$

Labor's total income is then compensation plus the fraction $\theta$ of proprietors' income. As a share of income net of taxes, it is

$$\frac{\text{compensation} + \theta\,\mathit{Prop}}{\text{GDI} - T} = \frac{\theta\,(\text{GDI} - T - \mathit{Prop}) + \theta\,\mathit{Prop}}{\text{GDI} - T} = \frac{\theta\,(\text{GDI} - T)}{\text{GDI} - T} = \theta.$$

So the labor share is $\theta$:

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: labor's share of income"}
$$\text{labor share} = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - \text{taxes on production} - \text{proprietors' income}} \tag{3}$$

The capital share is one minus the labor share. Fig. 3 uses equation (3).

**Islandia in numbers.** Take round numbers for one year: GDI of 100, taxes on production of 7, proprietors' income of 9 and compensation of 54 (in billions). Equation (3) gives a labor share of $54/84 \approx 0.643$, while the simple ratio compensation/GDI is only $0.54$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .mo-inwords title="In words: the self-employed"}
We cannot tell which part of the fisher's income pays for her work and which part pays for her boat. So we leave proprietors out of both the top and the bottom of the fraction. That gives the same answer as splitting their income in the same proportions as everybody else's.
:::

#### What the framework predicts

The identities say exactly which entries move when something happens. Some examples on Islandia, each worth $\$p$:

| Event | $C$ | $I$ | $G$ | $NX$ | GDP $Y$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| An islander buys a new boat built by Harbor Boatworks | $+p$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | $+p$ |
| An islander buys a new boat built on Mainland | $+p$ | 0 | 0 | $-p$ | 0 |
| Harbor Boatworks builds a new workshop | 0 | $+p$ | 0 | 0 | $+p$ |
| Harbor Boatworks builds boats it cannot sell this year | 0 | $+p$ (inventories) | 0 | 0 | $+p$ |
| A Mainland buyer purchases a new boat built on Islandia | 0 | 0 | 0 | $+p$ | $+p$ |
| The Islandia Treasury pays a pension | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| The Islandia Treasury hires a teacher | 0 | 0 | $+p$ | 0 | $+p$ |
| A dealer resells a used boat with margin $m$ | $+m$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | $+m$ |

- **Imports never add to GDP.** An imported boat enters $C$, $I$ or $G$ with a plus sign and $NX$ with a minus sign, and the two cancel.
- **The shares are tied together.** They add up to one, so their changes add up to zero (Step 4). If the consumption share rises over a decade, some other share must have fallen to make room.
- **GDP measures market production, not welfare.** It leaves out work done at home (cooking, caring for one's own children), the value of longer and healthier lives, leisure, and the using up of natural resources and harm to the environment. The note on Table 2.3 in the Fig. 3 section discusses a broader measure that adds some of them.

::: {.mo-takeaway}
Production, spending and income are three views of one total, so each dollar of GDP is counted once and earned once.
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-check title="Check your understanding"}
**1.** In Islandia's chain, the mill now buys grain worth \$40 and sells flour worth \$80, and the bakery still sells bread worth \$120. What is each producer's value added, and what is GDP?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The farm adds 40, the mill $80 - 40 = 40$ and the bakery $120 - 80 = 40$. By equation (1), GDP is $40 + 40 + 40 = 120$, the value of the bread. A higher price for flour moves value added from the bakery to the mill but leaves GDP unchanged.

</details>

**2.** An islander buys a new boat built on Mainland. Why does Islandia's GDP not change?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The boat raises consumption $C$ by its price, but it is also an import, so it lowers $NX = X - IM$ by the same amount. In equation (2) the two changes cancel. The boat was produced on Mainland, so it is part of Mainland's GDP, not Islandia's.

</details>
:::

### Real GDP: quantity indexes and chain weighting

#### Definitions

Islandia produces goods $i = 1, \dots, n$. Good $i$ has price $p_{i,t}$ and quantity $q_{i,t}$ in year $t$.

- **Nominal GDP** values each year's goods at that same year's prices: $\text{nominal GDP}_t = \sum_i p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t}$.
- **Real GDP at the prices of a base year $b$** values each year's goods at *one fixed* set of prices: $\sum_i p_{i,b}\,q_{i,t}$. Since the prices never change, it moves only when the quantities move. It is measured in "year-$b$ dollars".
- The **expenditure share** of good $i$ is $s_{i,t} \equiv p_{i,t}q_{i,t}\big/\sum_k p_{k,t}q_{k,t}$. In every year the shares add up to one.
- The **growth rate** of the quantity of good $i$ is $g_i$, so $q_{i,t+1} = (1+g_i)\,q_{i,t}$.

The **price level**, also called the **GDP deflator**, is defined as nominal GDP divided by real GDP, $P_t \equiv \text{nominal GDP}_t/\text{real GDP}_t$. Multiply both sides by real GDP:

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: the price level links nominal and real GDP"}
$$\text{nominal GDP}_t = P_t \times \text{real GDP}_t \tag{4}$$

Real GDP tracks only quantities, and the price level $P_t$ picks up the rest. If Islandia made just one good, $P_t$ would be its price and real GDP its quantity. In the base year real and nominal GDP coincide, so $P_b = 1$ (or 100, as an index).
:::

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: two ways to hold prices fixed.** To measure real growth from year $t$ to year $t+1$, we can value the quantities of both years at the *starting* prices (the **Laspeyres** index), or at the *ending* prices (the **Paasche** index):

$$1 + g^L = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t}}, \qquad 1 + g^P = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t}}.$$

**Step 2: Laspeyres growth is an average of the goods' growth rates.** In the top of the fraction, write $(1+g_i)\,q_{i,t}$ for $q_{i,t+1}$, and split the fraction into one term per good:

$$1 + g^L = \sum_i \frac{p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t}}{\sum_k p_{k,t}\,q_{k,t}}\,(1+g_i) = \sum_i s_{i,t}\,(1+g_i) = \sum_i s_{i,t} + \sum_i s_{i,t}\,g_i = 1 + \sum_i s_{i,t}\,g_i.$$

The last step uses the fact that the shares sum to one.

**Step 3: Paasche growth is an average too, with other weights.** Flip the Paasche fraction upside down and write $q_{i,t+1}/(1+g_i)$ for $q_{i,t}$:

$$\frac{1}{1+g^P} = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t}}{\sum_k p_{k,t+1}\,q_{k,t+1}} = \sum_i \frac{p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_k p_{k,t+1}\,q_{k,t+1}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+g_i} = \sum_i \frac{s_{i,t+1}}{1+g_i}.$$

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: the two indexes as weighted averages"}
$$g^L = \sum_i s_{i,t}\,g_i, \qquad \frac{1}{1+g^P} = \sum_i \frac{s_{i,t+1}}{1+g_i} \tag{5}$$

Both indexes average the growth rates of the individual goods. Laspeyres weights each good by its share of spending in the first year. Paasche uses the shares of the last year, in the form of a weighted *harmonic* mean of the growth factors.

**Islandia in numbers.** Suppose Islandia makes only apples and computers, as in the textbook's example. From 2026 to 2027 apples grow 10 percent and computers 20 percent. In 2026 computers take a share of about 0.833 of spending, so $g^L = 0.167\times 10\% + 0.833 \times 20\% \approx 18.3\%$. At the 2027 prices the Paasche rate is about 17.7%.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .mo-inwords title="In words: why the two indexes disagree"}
The weights depend on prices. On Islandia, computers got cheaper relative to apples while their quantity grew faster. At the old prices computers were still expensive, so the Laspeyres index gives the fast-growing good a big weight and reports more growth. At the new prices computers weigh less, and the Paasche index reports less.
:::

**When do the two agree?** (a) If every quantity grows at the same rate $g$, both formulas in (5) give exactly $g$, since the shares sum to one. (b) If every price changes by the same factor $\lambda$, so that $p_{i,t+1} = \lambda p_{i,t}$, then $\lambda$ cancels from the top and the bottom of the Paasche fraction, and it turns into the Laspeyres fraction. So the two indexes can differ only when **relative prices** change. Usually the goods whose relative price falls, like computers, are also the goods whose quantity grows fastest. At the starting prices those goods are still expensive and carry a large weight, so $g^L > g^P$. The longer the period, the more relative prices change, and the wider the gap.

**Step 4: chain weighting.** The chain-weighted index splits the difference and averages the two growth rates:

$$g^{\text{chain}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(g^L + g^P\right).$$

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: chain-weighted growth"}
$$g^{\text{chain}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(g^L + g^P\right) \tag{6}$$

Statistical agencies use the **Fisher** index, the geometric mean of the two growth factors, $1 + g^F = \sqrt{(1+g^L)(1+g^P)}$. When the two rates are close, the two kinds of average are practically the same ([Appendix C.6](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.6-approximations)); the code below compares them.

**Islandia in numbers.** Averaging 18.3% and 17.7% gives chain-weighted growth of about 18.0% from 2026 to 2027.
:::

**Step 5: linking the years into a chain.** Equation (6) is applied to each pair of neighboring years, so the weights are always the prices of those two years. To get levels from the growth rates, choose a **benchmark year** $b$ in which real GDP is set equal to nominal GDP. Then step forward and backward one year at a time:

$$X_{t+1} = X_t\,(1 + g^{\text{chain}}_{t,t+1}), \qquad X_t = \frac{X_{t+1}}{1 + g^{\text{chain}}_{t,t+1}},$$

where $X_t$ is chained real GDP. Across several years the growth factors multiply, $X_T = X_b\,(1+g_{b,b+1})(1+g_{b+1,b+2})\cdots(1+g_{T-1,T})$. The levels are reported in "chained year-$b$ dollars".

#### What the framework predicts

| From year $t$ to $t+1$ ... | Nominal GDP | Laspeyres $g^L$ | Paasche $g^P$ | Chained $g^{\text{chain}}$ | Price level $P$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| every price $\times\lambda$, same quantities | $\times\lambda$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | $\times\lambda$ |
| every quantity $\times\mu$, same prices | $\times\mu$ | $\mu-1$ | $\mu-1$ | $\mu-1$ | unchanged |
| relative prices change, same quantities | changes | 0 | 0 | 0 | moves with nominal GDP |
| quantities grow fastest where relative prices fall | rises | highest | lowest | in between | |

- **Real GDP ignores pure price changes.** When only prices move, every index reports zero real growth, and the whole change in nominal GDP lands in the price level.
- **Fixed base years go out of date.** Over long spans the Laspeyres index overstates growth and the Paasche index understates it. The U.S. national accounts moved to chain weighting in the 1990s, a time of fast-falling computer prices.
- **Chained components do not add up.** Each chained component has its own weights, so chained $C + I + G + NX$ is generally not equal to chained GDP. For **shares**, use nominal values, which do add up (equation 2). For **real growth rates**, use chained real values.

::: {.mo-takeaway}
Real GDP holds prices fixed so that only quantities move, and chain weighting keeps those prices up to date.
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-check title="Check your understanding"}
**1.** One year every price on Islandia doubles, and every quantity stays the same. What happens to nominal GDP, to real growth by each index, and to the price level?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Nominal GDP doubles. Relative prices do not change, so the Laspeyres, Paasche and chained indexes all report zero real growth (the first row of the table). By equation (4), the price level doubles: the whole change in nominal GDP is a change in prices.

</details>

**2.** Islandia's computers grew 20 percent and its apples 10 percent. Without computing anything, why must every index of real growth lie between these two numbers?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

By equation (5), the Laspeyres and Paasche rates are weighted averages of the goods' growth rates, with weights that are positive and sum to one. An average can never be larger than the largest item or smaller than the smallest. The chained rate of equation (6) averages the two again, so it lies in the same range.

</details>
:::

### Price indexes and inflation

#### Definitions

- The **GDP deflator** is the price level of equation (4), $P_t = \text{nominal GDP}_t/\text{real GDP}_t$, usually multiplied by 100 so that it equals 100 in the base year.
- The **inflation rate** is the growth rate of the price level, $\pi_{t+1} \equiv P_{t+1}/P_t - 1$.
- Each quantity index has a twin **price index**. The Laspeyres price index prices the *starting* quantities at both years' prices, $\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t}\big/\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t}$. The Paasche price index uses the *ending* quantities, $\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t+1}\big/\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}$.

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: nominal growth splits exactly into a price part and a quantity part.** Multiply and divide the growth factor of nominal GDP by $\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}$:

$$\frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t}} = \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}}}_{\text{Paasche price index}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t}}}_{\text{Laspeyres quantity index}}.$$

Multiplying and dividing by $\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t}$ instead gives the Laspeyres price index times the Paasche quantity index. Multiply the two splits together and take the square root: the Fisher price index times the Fisher quantity index is also exactly the growth factor of nominal GDP. That is why a chained price index and chained real GDP always satisfy equation (4).

**Step 2: the growth rate of a product.** Write equation (4) for two neighboring years and divide one by the other. The growth factor of a product is the product of the growth factors:

$$1 + g_{\text{nominal}} = (1+\pi)(1+g_{\text{real}}) = 1 + \pi + g_{\text{real}} + \pi\,g_{\text{real}}.$$

Take 1 away from both sides: $g_{\text{nominal}} = \pi + g_{\text{real}} + \pi\,g_{\text{real}}$. The last term multiplies two small numbers, so it is much smaller than the others. Dropping it ([Appendix C.5](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.5-growth-rates-and-the-growth-rules)) leaves

$$g_{\text{nominal GDP}} \approx \pi + g_{\text{real GDP}}.$$

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: nominal growth = inflation + real growth"}
$$g_{\text{nominal GDP}} \approx \pi + g_{\text{real GDP}} \tag{7}$$

To get inflation from the other two, solve the exact form for $\pi$: $\pi = (1+g_{\text{nominal}})/(1+g_{\text{real}}) - 1 \approx g_{\text{nominal}} - g_{\text{real}}$. In natural logs the split is exact: $\ln(\text{nominal GDP}) = \ln P + \ln(\text{real GDP})$, so the changes in logs add up with no error ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)).

**Islandia in numbers.** From 2026 to 2027 Islandia's nominal GDP grows 27.5% and chained real GDP 18.0%. The rule of thumb puts inflation at $27.5 - 18.0 = 9.5$ percent, but the exact formula gives about 8.0%.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .mo-inwords title="In words: more expensive goods, or more goods"}
Islandia's nominal GDP can grow because each apple and each computer costs more, or because there are more apples and computers. Equation (7) simply adds the two sources. The small cross term it leaves out is the price increase on the extra goods.
:::

**Step 3: rates over different periods.** With quarterly data, the change from a year ago compares a quarter with the same quarter one year before, $P_t/P_{t-4} - 1$. A one-quarter change becomes an **annual rate** by compounding it four times, $(P_t/P_{t-1})^4 - 1$, which is close to four times the quarterly rate when that rate is small ([Appendix C.3](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.3-exponents-and-exponential-growth)). Over $T$ years, the **average annual growth rate** $\bar{g}$ is the constant rate that carries the first value to the last: $P_T = P_0(1+\bar{g})^T$. Raise both sides of $P_T/P_0 = (1+\bar{g})^T$ to the power $1/T$ and subtract 1:

$$\bar{g} = \left(\frac{P_T}{P_0}\right)^{1/T} - 1.$$

(Here the bar marks an average over the years, not a parameter.)

**Step 4: changing the base year.** Rebasing an index to year $b$ means $P'_t = 100 \times P_t/P_b$. The constant $100/P_b$ cancels in every ratio, $P'_{t+1}/P'_t = P_{t+1}/P_t$, so rebasing shifts the level of the index but leaves every growth rate and inflation rate as it was.

#### What the framework predicts

Take the change in logs of equation (4), $\Delta\ln(\text{nominal GDP}) = \Delta\ln P + \Delta\ln(\text{real GDP})$: the **elasticity** of nominal GDP with respect to the price level is 1, and with respect to real GDP it is also 1.

| If ... | then ... |
|---|---|
| inflation is 1 point higher and real growth is unchanged | nominal growth is about 1 point higher |
| nominal growth is unchanged and real growth is 1 point higher | measured inflation is about 1 point lower |
| an index is rebased | its level changes; growth rates and inflation do not |

- **The rule of thumb in equation (7) works well when rates are small.** With 2 percent inflation and 2 percent real growth, the cross term is only $0.02 \times 0.02 = 0.0004$, or 0.04 percentage points. In Islandia's apples-and-computers example, with prices up 8 percent and quantities up 18 percent, it is about 1.5 points (see the checks below). In a country with very high inflation it can be large.
- **Ratio scales show inflation directly.** Since $\ln P_t$ rises by about $\pi$ each year, constant inflation draws a straight line on a ratio (log) scale (Fig. 4).

::: {.mo-takeaway}
Nominal growth is roughly inflation plus real growth; the small cross term matters only when rates are large.
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-check title="Check your understanding"}
**1.** Islandia's nominal GDP grows 5 percent in a year and its real GDP 3 percent. What is inflation by the rule of thumb, and what is it exactly?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

By equation (7), $\pi \approx 5 - 3 = 2$ percent. The exact form gives $\pi = 1.05/1.03 - 1 \approx 1.94\%$. With rates this small the cross term is tiny, so the rule of thumb is close.

</details>

**2.** Islandia's price level doubles over 10 years. What is the average annual inflation rate, and why is it not simply 10 percent?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

By Step 3, $\bar{g} = 2^{1/10} - 1 \approx 7.18\%$ a year. Ten years at 10 percent would multiply prices by $1.1^{10} \approx 2.59$, not by 2, because each year's increase builds on the higher prices of the year before.

</details>
:::

### Comparing countries: exchange rates and purchasing power parity

#### Definitions

Islandia's statisticians will also ask whether their island is richer or poorer than Mainland, which uses a different currency. The tools are the same for any pair of countries. We write them for the textbook's pair, China and the United States, and use its numbers.

- The **exchange rate** $e$ is the number of yuan that buy one dollar in the currency market.
- China's GDP in its own currency is $Y^{\text{yuan}}$. Converted at the exchange rate, it is $\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} = Y^{\text{yuan}}/e$.
- $\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}$ and $\text{price level}_{\text{China}}$ are the cost of the same basket of goods in each country, both in dollars at the exchange rate. Their ratio, the **relative price level**, says how expensive China is compared with the United States.
- The **PPP conversion factor** is the number of yuan that buy in China what one dollar buys in the United States: $\text{PPP} = e \times \text{price level}_{\text{China}}/\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}$.

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: China's real output.** Equation (4) holds in China too, with every value in dollars. Solve it for real GDP:

$$\text{real GDP}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}}.$$

**Step 2: value China's goods at U.S. prices.** To compare like with like, we price China's quantities at the prices that hold in the United States:

$$\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}} \times \text{real GDP}_{\text{China}}.$$

**Step 3: substitute Step 1 into Step 2.**

$$\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}} \times \text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}}.$$

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: GDP at common prices"}
$$\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}} \times \text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} \tag{8}$$

Dollar GDP is divided by China's relative price level. Where goods are cheap, the same dollars stand for more goods.

**In numbers.** With the textbook's 2019 data, 95.1 trillion yuan at 6.91 yuan per dollar is about \$13.8 trillion, 67 percent of U.S. GDP of \$20.6 trillion. Chinese prices are 68.4 percent of U.S. prices, so at U.S. prices China's GDP is about \$20.1 trillion, 98 percent of U.S. GDP.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .mo-inwords title="In words: cheap haircuts"}
Suppose a haircut on Islandia costs half of what it costs on Mainland. Converting Islandia's GDP at the exchange rate counts each Islandia haircut as half a Mainland haircut, even though it is the same service. Valuing both islands' goods at the same prices fixes this, and it raises the measured output of the cheaper place.
:::

**Step 4: the shortcut through the PPP factor.** Put $\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} = Y^{\text{yuan}}/e$ into (8) and gather the terms in the denominator:

$$\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{Y^{\text{yuan}}}{e \times \text{price level}_{\text{China}}/\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}} = \frac{Y^{\text{yuan}}}{\text{PPP}}.$$

So we can bypass the exchange rate entirely: GDP in yuan divided by the PPP conversion factor is GDP at U.S. prices.

**Step 5: how much of the gap is due to prices?** Divide (8) by U.S. GDP and take logs ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)):

$$\ln\frac{\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}}}{\text{GDP}_{\text{U.S.}}} = \ln\frac{\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}}}{\text{GDP}_{\text{U.S.}}} - \ln\frac{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}.$$

The log gap at common prices is the log gap at the exchange rate minus the log of the relative price level. When China is cheaper, that log is negative, and the gap at common prices is smaller. Dividing both GDPs by population gives the same split for GDP per person.

Pricing China's goods at U.S. prices is the cross-country cousin of a Laspeyres index; pricing U.S. goods at Chinese prices would be the Paasche version. In practice, the World Bank's International Comparison Program and the Penn World Table use average world prices ("international dollars"), much as chain weighting averages the two indexes over time.

#### What the framework predicts

| A 1% rise in ... | GDP at the exchange rate | GDP at common prices | Relative price level of China |
|---|---|---|---|
| the exchange rate $e$ (a weaker yuan), with yuan prices unchanged | $-1\%$ | 0 | $-1\%$ |
| every yuan price in China, with quantities unchanged | $+1\%$ | 0 | $+1\%$ |
| China's output of every good | $+1\%$ | $+1\%$ | 0 |

- **Common prices do not react to the currency market.** A swing in the exchange rate moves GDP in dollars one for one, but leaves the comparison at common prices where it was, because China's goods get cheaper in dollars by the same 1 percent (the elasticity of dollar GDP with respect to $e$ is $-1$).
- **Rich countries look less far ahead at common prices.** Services that cannot be traded, such as haircuts or restaurant meals, take a lot of labor, so they are cheap where wages are low. Poor countries therefore have low price levels, and comparisons at exchange rates exaggerate the income gaps between rich and poor countries.

::: {.mo-takeaway}
To compare countries, value their goods at the same prices; exchange rates alone make cheap countries look poorer than they are.
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-check title="Check your understanding"}
**1.** Suppose that at the exchange rate Islandia's GDP is 40 percent of Mainland's, and that goods on Islandia cost 80 percent of what they cost on Mainland. How large is Islandia's GDP at Mainland's prices, as a share of Mainland's GDP?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

By equation (8), divide the share at the exchange rate by the relative price level: $40/0.8 = 50$ percent. Because Islandia is cheaper, the gap shrinks from 60 to 50 percentage points.

</details>

**2.** Islandia's currency loses value against Mainland's, while nothing else changes on either island. What happens to Islandia's GDP at the exchange rate and at common prices?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

At the exchange rate, Islandia's GDP falls in Mainland's currency, one for one with the currency (the first row of the table). At common prices nothing changes: the same goods are produced, and Islandia's relative price level falls by exactly as much, so the two effects cancel in equation (8).

</details>
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-recap title="Recap"}
- **One total, three ways:** value added, final spending and income all add up to GDP, equations (1) and (2); the spending shares move together ([Fig. 2](#fig.-2-expenditure-shares-of-u.s.-gdp)).
- **Labor's share** leaves taxes and proprietors' income out of the denominator, equation (3) ([Fig. 3](#fig.-3-labors-share-of-gdp)).
- **Real GDP** values quantities at fixed prices; Laspeyres and Paasche are weighted averages of the goods' growth rates, and chain weighting averages the two, equations (5) and (6).
- **Prices and inflation:** nominal GDP is the price level times real GDP, equation (4), and nominal growth is about inflation plus real growth, equation (7) ([Fig. 4](#fig.-4-the-level-of-the-gdp-deflator); Fig. 5 plots the inflation rate).
- **Comparing countries** needs common prices, equation (8): at exchange rates, poor countries look poorer than they are ([Comparing countries](#comparing-countries-exchange-rates-and-purchasing-power-parity)).
:::

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with a precomputed slider or menu.
The next helpers build those versions. Run them and move on.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. changes_chart
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "base_year"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig
```

The data figures of this chapter let you add other countries. On the website, a menu above each of these
figures adds a group of countries (the G7, a world region, ...); the next cell builds those menus.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Helpers for the website's country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_traces(data, y, skip, x="year", fmt=".1f", markers=False):
    """One line per country of a long table, leaving out the countries in `skip`.

    Arguments
        data    : a long table with one row per country and year (columns country, x, y)
        y       : the column to draw
        skip    : the countries to leave out
        x       : the column on the horizontal axis
        fmt     : the number format of the hover text, e.g. ".1f"
        markers : True to draw a dot at every point of the line
    Returns
        a dictionary: each country's name and its list of traces (one line in its color)
    """
    # Step 1: go through the table one country at a time
    extra = {}
    for name, part in data.groupby("country"):
        if name not in skip:
            # Step 2: one line for this country, in its COLORS color, with hover text
            extra[name] = [go.Scatter(x=part[x], y=part[y], name=name,
                                      mode="lines+markers" if markers else "lines",
                                      line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=2),
                                      hovertemplate=f"<b>{name}</b><br>%{{x}}: %{{y:{fmt}}}<extra></extra>")]
    return extra


def country_menu(fig, extra, countries):
    """Add the extra countries' lines hidden, and a menu that shows one group of them.

    The groups are the G7, the G20, the OECD and each world region. The traces already in
    fig (the textbook's) stay as they are, and the slider steps only switch those.

    Arguments
        fig       : a Plotly figure with the textbook's countries
        extra     : the other countries' lines, from country_traces
        countries : a table with one row per country (columns country, region, g7, g20, oecd)
    Returns
        the same figure, with the extra lines hidden and the group menu above the plot
    """
    # Step 1: add every extra line, hidden, and remember whose line it is
    n = len(fig.data)                           # the number of textbook traces
    owner = []
    for name, traces in extra.items():
        for trace in traces:
            trace.visible = False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(name)
    # Step 2: the groups of the menu: G7, G20, OECD, then each region, A to Z
    groups = {"G7": countries.country[countries.g7], "G20": countries.country[countries.g20],
              "OECD": countries.country[countries.oecd]}
    for region in sorted(countries.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = countries.country[countries.region == region]
    # Step 3: one button per group; each switches only the extra lines, `rest`
    rest, autoscale = list(range(n, len(fig.data))), {"yaxis.autorange": True}
    buttons = [dict(label="Textbook only", method="update",
                    args=[{"visible": [False] * len(owner)}, autoscale, rest])]
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in set(members) for o in owner]
        # leave out a group with no country in the data
        if any(visible):
            buttons.append(dict(label=f"+ {label} ({sum(visible)})", method="update",
                                args=[{"visible": visible}, autoscale, rest]))
    # Step 4: put the menu above the plot, at the right
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=0, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    # Step 5: make every slider step switch only the textbook traces, the first n
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        for step in slider.steps:
            step.args = [{"visible": list(step.args[0]["visible"])}, step.args[1], list(range(n))]
    return fig
```

The last helper is like `slider_figure`, but with a dropdown menu, for the figures that show one country at a
time.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Helper for the website's one-country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Like slider_figure, but with a dropdown menu: one precomputed figure per value.

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. composition_chart
        name        : the argument the menu sets, e.g. "country"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute (e.g. the countries)
        start       : the value shown first
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a menu that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[values.index(start)].layout)
    # Step 2: copy every trace into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (values[i] == start)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one menu entry per value: its traces, title, labels, shapes and axes
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes],
                  "yaxis": f.layout.yaxis.to_plotly_json(),
                  "xaxis": f.layout.xaxis.to_plotly_json()}
        # a second vertical axis (Fig. 2)
        if "yaxis2" in f.layout.to_plotly_json():
            layout["yaxis2"] = f.layout.yaxis2.to_plotly_json()
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    # Step 4: put the menu above the plot, at the right
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=values.index(start), x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02,
                yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig
```

### The model as functions

This chapter has no behavior to model, but its measurement rules are formulas, and we write each one as a Python
*function*: a named recipe that takes inputs and gives back a result. The first three are shares, the value of
production, and chain-weighted growth, equation (6).

```{python}
# `def` creates a function. Its inputs are the arguments in parentheses, and
# `return` gives back the result. The text in triple quotes describes the function.
def share(part, total):
    """Share of a part in a total, in percent.

    Tables 2.1 and 2.2, and the shares of equation (2):  share = 100 * part / total

    Arguments
        part  : the part, e.g. consumption or compensation
        total : the total, e.g. GDP
    Returns
        the share of the part in the total, in percent
    """
    return 100 * part / total


def gdp_value(prices, quantities):
    """Value of production: price times quantity, added over all goods.

    Equation (4) and the indexes of equation (5) use it:  value = sum over i of p_i * q_i
    With each year's own prices it is nominal GDP; with fixed prices, real GDP.

    Arguments
        prices     : the price of each good, p_i
        quantities : the quantity of each good, q_i
    Returns
        the value of production, in dollars
    """
    # multiply good by good; `.sum()` adds up all the values of a column or a row
    return (prices * quantities).sum()


def chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche):
    """Chain-weighted growth of real GDP.

    Equation (6):  g_chain = (g_L + g_P) / 2

    Arguments
        g_laspeyres : the Laspeyres growth rate, g_L (at the starting prices)
        g_paasche   : the Paasche growth rate, g_P (at the ending prices)
    Returns
        the chain-weighted growth rate, g_chain
    """
    # the simple average of the two growth rates
    return (g_laspeyres + g_paasche) / 2
```

The last two functions compare countries. One converts GDP into dollars at the market exchange rate, and the
other values it at U.S. prices, equation (8).

```{python}
def to_dollars(gdp_local, exchange_rate):
    """GDP in dollars at the market exchange rate.

    The first step of equation (8):  GDP in dollars = GDP in local currency / e

    Arguments
        gdp_local     : GDP in the local currency, e.g. trillions of yuan
        exchange_rate : the exchange rate e, units of local currency per dollar
    Returns
        GDP in dollars
    """
    return gdp_local / exchange_rate


def at_common_prices(gdp_dollars, relative_price_level):
    """Real GDP at U.S. prices.

    Equation (8):  real GDP at U.S. prices = GDP in dollars / (price level / U.S. price level)

    Arguments
        gdp_dollars          : GDP in dollars, from to_dollars
        relative_price_level : the country's price level relative to the U.S. (U.S. = 1)
    Returns
        real GDP at U.S. prices, in dollars
    """
    # where goods are cheap (a relative price level below 1), the same dollars buy more
    return gdp_dollars / relative_price_level
```

<!-- cell -->

### Checking the key results

The rules came from algebra. Now we check them with numbers, one Key result at a time, mostly with small
made-up examples from Islandia.

**Check 1: value added adds up to final sales (equation 1).** Islandia's chain of three producers: a farm
grows grain worth \$40 and sells it to a mill; the mill turns it into flour worth \$70 and sells it to a bakery;
the bakery sells bread worth \$120 to islanders.

```{python}
# Step 1: each producer's sales and purchases. `pd.Series({...})` builds one
# labeled column from a dictionary: the keys become the labels.
revenue = pd.Series({"farm": 40, "mill": 70, "bakery": 120})
# each buys the output of the one before
inputs = pd.Series({"farm": 0, "mill": 40, "bakery": 70})
# Step 2: value added; subtracting two Series subtracts the values with the same label
value_added = revenue - inputs
print(value_added)
# Step 3: equation (1): the sum of value added equals the final sales
print(f"Sum of value added:   ${value_added.sum()}")
print(f"Final sales (bread):  ${revenue['bakery']}")
print(f"Sum of all revenues:  ${revenue.sum()}   (counts the grain three times and the flour twice)")
```

**Check 2: the labor share (equation 3).** We take made-up round numbers for one year's income on Islandia (in
billions) and check the algebra of Step 5: splitting proprietors' income in the economy-wide proportion gives
the same labor share as leaving it out of the fraction.

```{python}
# Step 1: Islandia's income in one year, in billions
gdi, taxes, proprietors, compensation = 100.0, 7.0, 9.0, 54.0
# Step 2: the labor share in two ways
theta = compensation / (gdi - taxes - proprietors)                  # equation (3)
# proprietors' income split by theta
split = (compensation + theta * proprietors) / (gdi - taxes)
# Step 3: both give the same share; compensation / GDI alone is too low
print(f"Labor share, equation (3):                 {theta:.4f}")
print(f"Labor share with proprietors split:        {split:.4f}")
print(f"Simple share, compensation / GDI:          {compensation / gdi:.4f}   (lower)")
```

**Check 3: real GDP in the economy of Table 2.4.** In this example Islandia produces only apples and computers,
as in the textbook's Table 2.4. We store its prices and quantities in two small tables, one row per year.

```{python}
# Prices and quantities of the two goods, one row per year.
# `pd.DataFrame({...}, index=[...])` builds a table from a dictionary: each key
# becomes a column, and the `index` gives the row labels.
prices = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [1, 2, 3], "computers": [900, 1000, 1000]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])
quantities = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [500, 500, 550], "computers": [5, 5, 6]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])
prices
```

Nominal GDP uses each year's own prices. Real GDP holds the prices fixed. The **Laspeyres** index measures the
change from 2026 to 2027 with the *initial* (2026) prices, and the **Paasche** index with the *final* (2027)
prices. **Chain weighting** averages the two growth rates (equation 6).

```{python}
# Step 1: nominal GDP, each year at its own prices. `prices.loc[2026]` picks the
# row for 2026. An f-string, f"... {x:,.0f}", puts a value into the text: ","
# adds thousands separators, ".0f" shows no decimals, ".1%" a percentage.
for year in [2025, 2026, 2027]:
    print(f"Nominal GDP in {year}: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[year], quantities.loc[year]):,.0f}")

# Step 2: growth 2026-2027, nominal and at fixed prices; multiplying two rows,
# `prices.loc[2026] * quantities.loc[2027]`, multiplies the matching columns
g_nominal = gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
# Laspeyres: at the 2026 prices; Paasche: at the 2027 prices
g_laspeyres = gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_paasche = gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_chain = chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche)              # equation (6)
# Step 3: the numbers of Table 2.4
print(f"Real GDP in 2027 at 2026 prices: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]):,.0f}")
print(f"Real GDP in 2026 at 2027 prices: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2026]):,.0f}")
print(f"Growth 2026-2027: nominal {g_nominal:.1%}, Laspeyres {g_laspeyres:.1%}, "
      f"Paasche {g_paasche:.1%}, chain-weighted {g_chain:.1%}")
# Step 4: chained real GDP in 2026, going back one year from 2027 (nominal GDP $7,650)
print(f"Chained real GDP in 2026, benchmarked to 2027: ${7650 / (1 + g_chain):,.0f}")
# the rule of thumb of equation (7)
print(f"Inflation (nominal growth minus real growth):  {g_nominal - g_chain:.1%}")
```

These are the numbers of Table 2.4: real growth is 18.3 percent at 2026 prices, 17.7 percent at 2027 prices,
and 18.0 percent chain-weighted. Nominal GDP grew 27.5 percent, so by the rule of thumb in equation (7) prices
rose by about $27.5 - 18.0 = 9.5$ percent. (The textbook gets \$6,483 for chained real GDP in 2026, because it
rounds the growth rate to 18.0 percent first; with the unrounded rate we get \$6,482.)

**Check 4: the two indexes as weighted averages (equation 5).** Apples grew 10 percent and computers 20
percent. Weighting these rates with the 2026 spending shares must give the Laspeyres rate, and the harmonic
form with the 2027 shares must give the Paasche rate. If every price rises by the same factor, the two indexes
must agree.

```{python}
# Step 1: prices and quantities of the two years, and the spending shares
p0, p1 = prices.loc[2026], prices.loc[2027]
q0, q1 = quantities.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]
s0 = p0 * q0 / gdp_value(p0, q0)                 # spending shares in 2026
s1 = p1 * q1 / gdp_value(p1, q1)                 # spending shares in 2027
growth_i = q1 / q0 - 1                           # growth of each good's quantity
# Step 2: equation (5), both sides for each index
print(f"Shares of computers: {s0['computers']:.3f} in 2026, {s1['computers']:.3f} in 2027")
print(f"Laspeyres: direct {g_laspeyres:.4%}   share-weighted average {(s0 * growth_i).sum():.4%}")
print(f"Paasche:   direct {g_paasche:.4%}   harmonic form          {1 / (s1 / (1 + growth_i)).sum() - 1:.4%}")
# Step 3: every price 50% higher, so relative prices are unchanged
p_scaled = 1.5 * p0
g_scaled = gdp_value(p_scaled, q1) / gdp_value(p_scaled, q0) - 1
print(f"Paasche when all prices rise by the same factor: {g_scaled:.4%} (= Laspeyres)")
```

The price of apples rose by half while computers kept their price, so computers became relatively cheaper, and
their quantity grew faster. At the 2026 prices computers carry more weight, which is why the Laspeyres rate is
the higher one.

**Check 5: the exact split of nominal growth, and the Fisher index.** Step 1 of the price block says that a
price index times the matching quantity index gives the growth factor of nominal GDP exactly. Step 2 says that
the rule of thumb in equation (7) misses the cross term $\pi\,g$.

```{python}
# Step 1: the price indexes; `x ** 0.5` is the square root of x (Fisher)
price_laspeyres = gdp_value(p1, q0) / gdp_value(p0, q0)
price_paasche = gdp_value(p1, q1) / gdp_value(p0, q1)
price_fisher = (price_laspeyres * price_paasche) ** 0.5
g_fisher = ((1 + g_laspeyres) * (1 + g_paasche)) ** 0.5 - 1
# Step 2: each price index times the matching quantity index gives nominal growth
print(f"Nominal growth factor:                     {1 + g_nominal:.5f}")
print(f"Paasche price x Laspeyres quantity:        {price_paasche * (1 + g_laspeyres):.5f}")
print(f"Laspeyres price x Paasche quantity:        {price_laspeyres * (1 + g_paasche):.5f}")
print(f"Fisher price x Fisher quantity:            {price_fisher * (1 + g_fisher):.5f}")
print(f"Real growth: chain-weighted {g_chain:.4%}, Fisher {g_fisher:.4%}")
# Step 3: exact inflation, (1 + pi) = (1 + nominal growth) / (1 + real growth)
exact = (1 + g_nominal) / (1 + g_chain) - 1
print(f"Inflation: rule of thumb {g_nominal - g_chain:.2%}, exact {exact:.2%}, "
      f"Fisher price index {price_fisher - 1:.2%}")
# Step 4: the cross term pi * g that equation (7) leaves out
print(f"Cross term pi x g: {exact * g_chain:.2%}  ->  {exact:.2%} + {g_chain:.2%} + {exact * g_chain:.2%} "
      f"= {exact + g_chain + exact * g_chain:.2%}")
```

The four products agree to the last digit, and the arithmetic and geometric averages of the two growth rates
differ only in the third decimal. But with rates this large, the rule of thumb is off: prices in this economy
rose by about 8.0 percent, not 9.5. The missing 1.5 points are the cross term.

**Check 6: rates over different periods.** A price level that rises 1 percent every quarter rises by more than
4 percent a year, because the increases compound. And a price level that doubles in 10 years grows at an
average annual rate of $2^{1/10} - 1$.

```{python}
# Step 1: 1% a quarter, compounded over four quarters
quarterly = 0.01
print(f"1% a quarter, compounded: {(1 + quarterly) ** 4 - 1:.4%} a year (simple rule: {4 * quarterly:.0%})")
# Step 2: the average annual growth rate when prices double in 10 years
g_bar = 2 ** (1 / 10) - 1
print(f"Prices double in 10 years: average growth {g_bar:.3%} a year")
print(f"Check: (1 + {g_bar:.5f})^10 = {(1 + g_bar) ** 10:.4f}")
```

**Check 7: China and the United States at common prices (equation 8).** We use the textbook's 2019 numbers:
U.S. GDP of \$20.6 trillion, China's GDP of 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar, and Chinese prices at
68.4 percent of U.S. prices.

```{python}
# China's GDP in dollars, then at U.S. prices, equation (8)
# 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar (2019)
china_dollars = to_dollars(95.1, 6.91)
# goods in China cost 68.4% of U.S. prices
china_ppp = at_common_prices(china_dollars, 0.684)
# both as a share of U.S. GDP, $20.6 trillion
print(f"China at the exchange rate: ${china_dollars:.1f} trillion, {china_dollars / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")
print(f"China at common prices:     ${china_ppp:.1f} trillion, {china_ppp / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")
```

With these numbers, China's economy looks like two-thirds of the U.S. economy at the exchange rate, but almost
exactly as large at common prices. The next cell checks Steps 4 and 5 and the first row of the table of
predictions: the PPP shortcut, the log split of the gap, and a 1 percent weaker yuan.

```{python}
# Step 1: the PPP shortcut, yuan that buy what one dollar buys in the U.S.
ppp = 6.91 * 0.684
print(f"PPP factor: {ppp:.3f} yuan per dollar; 95.1 / PPP = ${95.1 / ppp:.2f} trillion (= {china_ppp:.2f})")
# Step 2: the log split of the gap; `np.log` is the natural logarithm
gap_exchange, gap_prices = np.log(china_dollars / 20.6), np.log(0.684)
print(f"Log gap at the exchange rate {gap_exchange:.4f} - log relative price level {gap_prices:.4f} "
      f"= {gap_exchange - gap_prices:.4f};  log gap at common prices {np.log(china_ppp / 20.6):.4f}")
# Step 3: the yuan weakens by 1 percent
e_new = 6.91 * 1.01
dollars_new = to_dollars(95.1, e_new)
# China's relative price level falls with e
ppp_new = at_common_prices(dollars_new, ppp / e_new)
print(f"1% weaker yuan: GDP in dollars {dollars_new / china_dollars - 1:+.2%}, "
      f"at common prices {ppp_new / china_ppp - 1:+.2%}")
```

The log gap at common prices is close to zero, so China and the United States had almost the same GDP. A weaker
yuan makes China's GDP look about 1 percent smaller in dollars, while the comparison at common prices does not
move at all.

## Who buys GDP: the expenditure side

We first split GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports, and follow the shares of the four parts over time.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 1: Composition of U.S. GDP

**Goal.** See how the four spending shares of U.S. GDP have moved since 1929.

The file has one row per year and one column per share of GDP, in percent.

```{python}
shares = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig2-1.csv")
shares.tail()
```

The national income identity, equation (2), says the four shares must add up to 100 percent in every year. Let us check.

```{python}
total = shares.consumption_share + shares.investment_share + shares.government_share + shares.net_exports_share
print(f"C + I + G + NX, as a percent of GDP: between {total.min():.2f} and {total.max():.2f}")
```

The table is **wide**: one column per component. Plotly Express prefers **long** tables, with one row
per component and year.

> **Python note.** `.melt(id_vars="year")` turns the share columns into rows: the old column names go
> into a new column (`var_name`) and the numbers into another (`value_name`). `.map(NAMES)` then replaces
> each column name with a readable name, using the dictionary `NAMES`.

```{python}
NAMES = {"net_exports_share": "Net exports", "consumption_share": "Consumption",
         "investment_share": "Investment", "government_share": "Government purchases"}
long = shares.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="series", value_name="share")
long["component"] = long.series.map(NAMES)
long.head()
```

<!-- cell -->

#### The same accounts for other countries

The World Bank publishes the same four shares for about 190 countries, in `expenditure_world.csv`
(from 1960 for many). A second file, `countries.csv`, lists every economy with its world region and its
membership of the G7, the G20 and the OECD; the website's country menus use it.

```{python}
world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "expenditure_world.csv")
countries = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
world[world.country == "China"].tail(3)
```

The World Bank follows the United Nations' *System of National Accounts*, which draws one line
differently from the BEA: what governments spend on roads, buildings and equipment counts as
**investment**, and government purchases cover only government *consumption*. Compare the U.S. numbers
of the two sources.

> **Python note.** `pd.DataFrame({...})` builds a table from several columns; their rows are matched by
> year. `.loc[[1970, 2000, 2024]]` keeps three years.

```{python}
bea = shares.set_index("year")
wb = world[world.country == "United States"].set_index("year")
pd.DataFrame({"I, BEA": bea.investment_share, "I, World Bank": wb.investment,
              "G, BEA": bea.government_share, "G, World Bank": wb.government}).loc[[1970, 2000, 2024]].round(1)
```

The World Bank's investment share is about 4 points higher and its government share about 4 points
lower: the same spending sits in a different box. Consumption and net exports agree. **Before you compare
countries, check that the numbers use the same definitions.**

The textbook stacks the shares on top of each other: net exports at the bottom, then consumption,
investment, and government purchases up to 100 percent. `px.area` stacks areas in the order of
`category_orders`, and `color_discrete_map` gives each component a fixed color. Because net exports are
negative in recent decades, consumption starts *below* zero in those years. The function draws the BEA's
U.S. data, or the World Bank's data for any other country.

> **Python note.** `np.floor` and `np.ceil` round down and up, so `10 * np.ceil(x / 10)` is the next
> multiple of 10 above `x`: the axes grow in steps of 10 points for countries with unusual shares.
> `data.groupby("year").share.sum()` adds up the four shares within each year (the top of the stack),
> and `max(a, b)` is the larger of two numbers.

```{python}
ORDER = ["Net exports", "Consumption", "Investment", "Government purchases"]
COLORS_GDP = {"Net exports": "#e0a33b", "Consumption": "#5aa0d8", "Investment": GREEN, "Government purchases": TEAL}
LABELS = {"year": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "component": "Component"}
WB_NAMES = {"consumption": "Consumption", "investment": "Investment", "government": "Government purchases",
            "net_exports": "Net exports"}
BEA = "United States (BEA)"


def composition_chart(style="stacked areas", country=BEA):
    """Fig. 2.1: the expenditure shares of GDP, stacked or as separate lines (BEA, or World Bank data)."""
    data = long
    title = "Since 1950: consumption ≈ 64%, government ≈ 20%, investment ≈ 17% of U.S. GDP"
    if country != BEA:
        data = world[world.country == country].melt(id_vars="year", value_vars=list(WB_NAMES), value_name="share")
        data["component"] = data.variable.map(WB_NAMES)
        title = f"Composition of GDP in {country} (World Bank definitions)"
    if style == "stacked areas":
        fig = px.area(data, x="year", y="share", color="component", color_discrete_map=COLORS_GDP,
                      category_orders={"component": ORDER}, labels=LABELS, title=title)
    else:
        fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="share", color="component", color_discrete_map=COLORS_GDP,
                      category_orders={"component": ORDER}, labels=LABELS, title=title)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    top = max(data.groupby("year").share.sum().max(), data.share.max())     # stacked total or largest share
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.year.min(), 2025])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[min(-10, 10 * np.floor(data.share.min() / 10)), max(100, 10 * np.ceil(top / 10))])
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** `interact` draws the figure again whenever you change a widget. `ToggleButtons`
> is a row of buttons, one per option, and a `Dropdown` is a menu from which you choose one entry. The `;`
> at the end only hides an extra line of text.

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(composition_chart,
         style=ToggleButtons(options=["stacked areas", "separate lines"], description="chart", style=WIDE),
         country=Dropdown(options=[BEA] + sorted(world.country.unique()), value=BEA, description="country"));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 1 with buttons for the chart style and a menu of countries (G20 and OECD)
members = countries[countries.g20 | countries.oecd].country
fig = dropdown_figure(composition_chart, "country", [BEA] + sorted(set(members) & set(world.country)), start=BEA)
fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [dict(type="buttons", direction="right", x=0, xanchor="left",
    y=1.02, yanchor="bottom", buttons=[dict(label="stacked areas", method="restyle", args=[{"stackgroup": "1"}]),
                                       dict(label="separate lines", method="restyle", args=[{"stackgroup": None}])])])
fig
```

**Sources.** Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, national accounts (NIPA Table 1.1.5), via FRED: [GDP (`GDPA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA),
[personal consumption expenditures (`PCECA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCECA), [gross private domestic investment (`GPDIA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GPDIA),
[government consumption expenditures and gross investment (`GCEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GCEA) and [net exports (`A019RC1A027NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A019RC1A027NBEA);
other countries: World Bank, World Development Indicators, shares of GDP: [household consumption (`NE.CON.PRVT.ZS`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.CON.PRVT.ZS),
[gross capital formation (`NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS), [government consumption (`NE.CON.GOVT.ZS`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.CON.GOVT.ZS) and [external balance on goods and services (`NE.RSB.GNFS.ZS`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.RSB.GNFS.ZS). Country groups: [World Bank country classifications](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups).
Prepared files: [`data/ch02/fig2-1.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch02/fig2-1.csv), [`data/ch02/expenditure_world.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch02/expenditure_world.csv) and [`data/ch02/countries.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch02/countries.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch02/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 2.1 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

The website's menu lists the G20 and OECD members; in Colab you can choose any of the countries.

**What to notice.**

- From 1950 on, the shares hardly move: consumption averages about 64 percent, government purchases
  about 20 percent and investment about 17 percent (see the numbers below).
- World War II stands out. In 1943–1944 government purchases took 48 percent of GDP, and consumption
  and investment were squeezed.
- During the Great Depression, investment collapsed to 3 percent of GDP in 1932, while the
  consumption share peaked at 82 percent.
- Net exports were zero or slightly positive for most years before 1976, and negative in every year
  since. The deficit was deepest in 2006. Hover over the lines to read the values, and click a
  component in the legend to hide it.
- Choose China: in 2024 consumption was only 40 percent of GDP and investment also 40 percent, about
  twice the U.S. investment share. Choose Ireland: in 2025 its net exports were 40 percent of GDP,
  because multinational firms book large exports there.

> **Python note.** `.set_index("year")` uses the years as row labels, so `by_year.loc[1950:]` keeps the
> rows from 1950 on. `.idxmax()` returns the row label (here the year) of the largest value, and
> `.idxmin()` that of the smallest.

```{python}
by_year = shares.set_index("year")
print("Average shares, 1950-2025 (percent):")
print(by_year.loc[1950:].mean().round(1))
print(f"Government purchases peaked at {by_year.government_share.max():.1f}% in {by_year.government_share.idxmax()}")
print(f"Investment fell to {by_year.investment_share.min():.1f}% in {by_year.investment_share.idxmin()}")
print(f"Deepest trade deficit: {by_year.net_exports_share.min():.1f}% in {by_year.net_exports_share.idxmin()}")
print(f"Last year with a trade surplus: {by_year[by_year.net_exports_share > 0].index.max()}")
```

#### Key numbers: Table 2.1, the expenditure approach

The textbook's Table 2.1 breaks down U.S. GDP in 2022 in more detail. A wider data file holds the
national accounts lines behind it, in billions of current dollars, for every year since 1929.

```{python}
nipa = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "nipa_annual.csv").set_index("year")
nipa.loc[2022]
```

The function below builds the table for any year. Population is in thousands, so GDP per person in
dollars is billions × 1,000,000 / population.

```{python}
EXPENDITURE = {"gdp": "Gross domestic product", "consumption": "Personal consumption expenditures",
               "motor_vehicles": "   Motor vehicles and parts", "food": "   Food", "housing": "   Housing",
               "medical": "   Medical care", "investment": "Gross private domestic investment",
               "structures": "   Structures (nonresidential)", "equipment": "   Equipment",
               "ipp": "   Intellectual property products", "residential": "   Residential",
               "government": "Government purchases", "defense": "   National defense",
               "net_exports": "Net exports of goods and services", "exports": "   Exports", "imports": "   Imports"}


def expenditure_table(year):
    """Table 2.1: the expenditure approach to U.S. GDP in one year."""
    row = nipa.loc[year, list(EXPENDITURE)]
    table = pd.DataFrame({"Trillions of dollars": row / 1000,
                          "Share of GDP (percent)": share(row, row["gdp"]),
                          "Per person (dollars)": row * 1_000_000 / nipa.loc[year, "population"]})
    table.index = list(EXPENDITURE.values())
    return table.round(1)
```

We put the textbook's shares next to ours, to compare.

```{python}
table_2022 = expenditure_table(2022)
table_2022["Textbook share"] = [100.0, 68.2, 2.7, 5.1, 11.8, 10.6, 18.0, 2.4, 5.1, 5.5, 4.3, 17.3, 3.5, -3.9, 11.8, 15.7]
table_2022
```

```{python}
gdp_2022 = nipa.loc[2022, "gdp"] / 1000
print(f"GDP in 2022: ${gdp_2022:.2f} trillion in our data, $25.5 trillion in the textbook "
      f"({gdp_2022 / 25.5 - 1:.1%} higher)")
```

Our numbers are close to the textbook's but not identical. This is a lesson about data: **national
accounts are revised**. In 2023 the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) did a comprehensive update
that raised the level of U.S. GDP in 2022 by about 2 percent, after the textbook's numbers were
collected. Shares change much less than levels: consumption is still about 68 percent of GDP,
investment about 18–19 percent and government purchases about 17 percent.

### Fig. 2: Expenditure shares of U.S. GDP

**Goal.** Zoom in on the years since 1970, when the consumption share started to rise.

```{python}
recent = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig2-2.csv")
recent = recent.rename(columns={"consumption_share": "Consumption", "investment_share": "Investment",
                                "government_share": "Government purchases", "net_exports_share": "Net exports"})
recent.head()
```

As in the textbook, consumption is measured on its own axis on the right, because it is much larger
than the other three shares. The function draws the BEA's U.S. data, or the World Bank's data (from
1970) for any other country; both axes widen in steps of 10 points when a country's shares do not fit.

> **Python note.** `px.line` with a list of columns as `y` draws one line per column. We then add the
> consumption line with `fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(...))`, and `yaxis="y2"` attaches it to a second
> vertical axis. In `update_layout`, `overlaying="y"` puts that axis on top of the first one, and
> `side="right"` puts its labels on the right. `.rename(columns=WB_NAMES)` gives the World Bank's
> columns the same names as ours, `data.iloc[0]` is the first row and `data.iloc[-1]` the last, and
> `"rose" if a > b else "fell"` picks one of two words.

```{python}
def shares_chart(country=BEA):
    """Fig. 2.2: expenditure shares since 1970, consumption on the right axis (BEA, or World Bank data)."""
    data = recent
    if country != BEA:
        data = world[(world.country == country) & (world.year >= 1970)].rename(columns=WB_NAMES)
    first, last = data.iloc[0], data.iloc[-1]
    verb = "rose" if last.Consumption > first.Consumption else "fell"
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y=["Government purchases", "Investment", "Net exports"],
                  color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, GREEN, "#e0a33b"],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Share of GDP (percent)", "variable": "Component"},
                  title=f"{country}: consumption {verb} from {first.Consumption:.0f}% to {last.Consumption:.0f}% "
                        f"of GDP, {first.year:.0f}–{last.year:.0f}")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=data.year, y=data.Consumption, name="Consumption (right axis)",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), yaxis="y2"))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    others = data[["Government purchases", "Investment", "Net exports"]]
    low, high = min(-6, 10 * np.floor(others.min().min() / 10)), max(46, 10 * np.ceil(others.max().max() / 10) + 20)
    c_low, c_high = min(36, 10 * np.floor(data.Consumption.min() / 10) - 30), max(70, 10 * np.ceil(data.Consumption.max() / 10))
    fig.update_layout(yaxis=dict(range=[low, high], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25] if high == 46 else None),
                      yaxis2=dict(title="Consumption (percent of GDP)", overlaying="y", side="right",
                                  range=[c_low, c_high], tickvals=[60, 64, 68] if c_low == 36 else None, showgrid=False),
                      legend=dict(x=1.1), xaxis=dict(range=[1969, 2026]))      # legend clear of the right axis
    return fig
```

```{python}
interact(shares_chart, country=Dropdown(options=[BEA] + sorted(since_1970.country.unique()), value=BEA, description="country"));
```

```{python}
wide = recent.set_index("year")
pd.DataFrame({"1970": wide.loc[1970], "2025": wide.loc[2025], "change": wide.loc[2025] - wide.loc[1970]}).round(1)
```

The consumption share rose from 60.3 percent in 1970 to 67.6 percent in 2025, and since 2010 it has
stayed between about 66.6 and 68.6 percent. The government share fell from 23.5 to 17.4 percent, and
net exports went from a small surplus to a deficit of 3.0 percent. Because the four shares always add
up to 100, **the four changes must add up to zero**: a rise in one share is always matched by falls in
others. The chart below shows the changes directly.

> **Python note.** `wide.loc[base_year:] - wide.loc[base_year]` subtracts one row from every row of the
> table, column by column. The result is the change of each share since the base year, in percentage points.
> `.reset_index()` turns the year labels back into an ordinary column, which `melt` and Plotly need.

```{python}
CHANGE_COLORS = {"Consumption": BLUE, "Investment": GREEN, "Government purchases": TEAL, "Net exports": "#e0a33b"}


def changes_chart(base_year=1970):
    """Fig. 2.2, second view: change in each expenditure share since base_year (percentage points)."""
    changes = (wide.loc[base_year:] - wide.loc[base_year]).reset_index()
    long_changes = changes.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="component", value_name="change")
    fig = px.line(long_changes, x="year", y="change", color="component", color_discrete_map=CHANGE_COLORS,
                  range_x=[1970, 2025], range_y=[-8, 10],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "change": f"Change since {base_year} (percentage points)",
                          "component": "Component"})
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    c = wide.loc[2025] - wide.loc[base_year]
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{base_year}–2025: C {c['Consumption']:+.1f}, I {c['Investment']:+.1f}, "
                            f"G {c['Government purchases']:+.1f}, NX {c['Net exports']:+.1f} points")
    return fig
```
