**What to notice.**

- Since 1970, the rise in the consumption share (+7.4 points) was matched mostly by the fall in
  government purchases (−6.2 points) and in net exports (−3.4 points). Investment ended a little higher.
- Investment is the most volatile share. It fell to 13.3 percent of GDP in 2009, during the Great
  Recession.
- Choose 2000 as the base year: the big shift into consumption happened before 2000 (only +1.6 points
  since then). With 2010 as the base, investment rises and government purchases fall by 3.6 points
  each, because 2010 came just after the Great Recession, when investment was low.
- In the first chart, choose China: its consumption share fell from 53 percent of GDP in 1970 to 35
  percent in 2010, while investment boomed; by 2024 it was back at 40 percent. Choose Japan: its
  consumption share rose from 45 to 53 percent.

## Who earns GDP: labor's share

The same GDP is also income. Here we ask how much of it goes to workers, and whether that share has really stayed constant.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 3: Labor's share of GDP

**Goal.** Check one of the classic "stylized facts" of macroeconomics: that labor earns about
two-thirds of GDP, year after year.

The income approach splits GDP into the income earned by workers (**compensation**: wages, salaries
and benefits) and the income earned by the owners of capital. Two parts need care. Taxes on
production (such as sales taxes) are income of neither, so they are left out. And the income of
the self-employed (**proprietors' income**) mixes both, so it is split between labor and capital in
the same proportion as in the rest of the economy. The result is

$$\text{labor share} = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - \text{taxes on production} - \text{proprietors' income}}$$

where GDI is gross domestic income, the income-side measure of GDP.

```{python}
labor = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig2-3.csv")
labor.tail()
```

We can rebuild this measure from the national accounts lines in `nipa`.

```{python}
rebuilt = nipa.compensation / (nipa.gdi - nipa.taxes_less_subsidies - nipa.proprietors_income)
print(f"Labor share in 2022: {rebuilt[2022]:.4f} rebuilt from nipa, "
      f"{labor[labor.year == 2022].labor_share.iloc[0]:.4f} in the figure file")
```

The labor share is a classic cross-country fact too. The Penn World Table, a database of national
accounts for about 180 countries, estimates it for 140 of them from 1950 on (`labor_share_world.csv`).
Its method differs a little from the textbook's: it treats the income of the self-employed in other
ways, depending on the data each country has. For the United States its share is about 0.03 lower.

```{python}
pwt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "labor_share_world.csv")
us_pwt = pwt[pwt.country == "United States"].set_index("year").labor_share
print(f"{pwt.country.nunique()} countries, {pwt.year.min()}-{pwt.year.max()}")
print(f"U.S. 2019: {us_pwt[2019]:.3f} in the Penn World Table, {labor.set_index('year').labor_share[2019]:.3f} in Fig. 3")
```

Each country keeps one color in every chart: a few have fixed colors, and the others take one of 24
distinct colors in turn.

> **Python note.** `for i, name in enumerate(...)` hands over each name together with its position `i`
> (0, 1, 2, ...). `i % 24` is the remainder after dividing by 24, so the 24 colors repeat in turn.
> `if name not in COLORS:` skips the names that already have a color.

```{python}
COLORS = {"United States": BLUE, "Germany": TEAL, "Japan": GREEN, "China": "#e0a33b", "United Kingdom": "#5aa0d8"}
OTHER = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24                 # 24 distinct colors for the other countries
for i, name in enumerate(countries.country):
    if name not in COLORS:
        COLORS[name] = OTHER[i % len(OTHER)]
```

The textbook points to a downward trend since about 1970. Our chart adds a straight trend line fitted to
the data: pick the year where the line starts, and see how steep the decline is. You can also add other countries from the Penn World Table
(including the United States, to compare the two measures).

> **Python note.** `np.polyfit(x, y, 1)` fits the best straight line $y = a + bx$ through the points
> (by least squares) and returns the slope $b$ first and the intercept $a$ second. `SelectMultiple` is a
> list from which you can pick several entries: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click to add or remove one.
> `.isin(chosen)` keeps the rows of the chosen countries, and `for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):`
> hands over each country's name and rows in turn, so each gets its own line. `pd.concat([a, b])` stacks
> two columns into one, and `x if condition else y` picks `x` when the condition is true.

```{python}
def labor_share_chart(start=1970, chosen=()):
    """Fig. 2.3: labor's share of GDP, 1950-2025, with a trend line from `start`; other countries from PWT."""
    after = labor[labor.year >= start]
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(after.year, after.labor_share, 1)
    fig = px.line(labor, x="year", y="labor_share", labels={"year": "Year", "labor_share": "Labor share of GDP"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), fill="tozeroy", fillcolor="rgba(22, 82, 140, 0.12)",
                      name="Labor share (textbook)", showlegend=True)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=after.year, y=intercept + slope * after.year, name=f"Trend since {start}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    extra = pwt[pwt.country.isin(chosen)]
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.year, y=part.labor_share, name=f"{name} (PWT)", line=dict(color=COLORS[name])))
    shown = pd.concat([labor.labor_share, extra.labor_share])      # every value on the chart
    low = 0.55 if shown.min() >= 0.55 else 0.05 * np.floor(shown.min() / 0.05)      # widen in steps of 0.05
    high = 0.75 if shown.max() <= 0.75 else 0.05 * np.ceil(shown.max() / 0.05)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1950, 2025])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high], tickvals=[0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.75] if low == 0.55 else None)  # no corner label
    # slope is per year, as a fraction: x 100 for percentage points, x 10 for a decade
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Labor share: trend since {start} is {1000 * slope:+.1f} percentage points per decade")
    return fig
```

         start=Dropdown(options=[1950, 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000], value=1970, description="trend from",
                        style=WIDE),
         chosen=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(pwt.country.unique()), value=(), rows=8, description="add (PWT)"));
```

```

(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch02/README.md)).

On the website, the menu above the chart adds a group of countries from the Penn World Table; click a
country in the legend to hide it.

```{python}
share_by_year = labor.set_index("year").labor_share
print(f"Average 1950-2025: {share_by_year.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Highest: {share_by_year.max():.3f} in {share_by_year.idxmax()}; lowest: {share_by_year.min():.3f} in {share_by_year.idxmin()}")
print(f"Average 1950-1969: {share_by_year.loc[1950:1969].mean():.3f}; average 2010-2025: {share_by_year.loc[2010:].mean():.3f}")
print("Years below 0.60:", list(share_by_year[share_by_year < 0.60].index))
```

**What to notice.**

- On average, labor earned 0.65 of income from 1950 to 2025, close to the two-thirds of the stylized
  fact. Until 2021 the share stayed between 0.60 and 0.70.
- But the share is not constant. It peaked at 0.69 in 1970 and has drifted down since: from 1970 the
  trend falls by about 1.3 percentage points per decade. Move the starting year to 1990 or 2000 and
  the decline looks even steeper.
- Since 2022 the share has been below 0.60 for the first time in these data (0.586 in 2025). Our values
  for the last years in the textbook are slightly lower than the book's, because of the 2023 data
  revision. Part of the decline reflects how the national accounts treat software and R&D, which is
  still debated by researchers.
- Add other countries. The labor share fell in Germany too (0.69 in 1970, 0.64 in 2023), but it rose in
  Japan (0.51 to 0.59) and South Korea (0.42 to 0.55). Two-thirds is a rough rule for rich countries,
  not a law of nature. Oil exporters such as Qatar (0.18) and Kuwait (0.25) have very low shares,
  because most of their income is oil revenue. Some values are doubtful: the Penn World Table puts
  Venezuela at exactly 0.0844 in every year from 2019 to 2023, a value carried forward, not measured. **Look at the extremes before you trust
  a cross-country file.**

#### Key numbers: Table 2.2, the income approach

```{python}
INCOME = {"gdp": "Gross domestic product", "compensation": "Compensation of employees",
          "wages": "   Wages and salaries", "benefits": "   Benefits",
          "taxes_less_subsidies": "Taxes less subsidies on businesses",
          "net_operating_surplus": "Net operating surplus of businesses",
          "depreciation": "Depreciation of fixed capital"}


def income_table(year):
    """Table 2.2: the income approach to U.S. GDP in one year."""
    row = nipa.loc[year, list(INCOME)]
    table = pd.DataFrame({"Trillions of dollars": row / 1000,
                          "Share of GDP (percent)": share(row, row["gdp"]),
                          "Per person (dollars)": row * 1_000_000 / nipa.loc[year, "population"]})
    table.index = list(INCOME.values())
    return table.round(1)


income_2022 = income_table(2022)
income_2022["Textbook share"] = [100.0, 53.2, 43.9, 9.3, 6.5, 23.5, 16.8]
income_2022
```

Compensation, taxes, the operating surplus and depreciation should add up to total income. They do,
but to **gross domestic income** (GDI) rather than to GDP. The two differ by a small *statistical
discrepancy*, because the BEA measures spending and income from different sources.

```{python}
y = nipa.loc[2022]
income_sum = y.compensation + y.taxes_less_subsidies + y.net_operating_surplus + y.depreciation
print(f"Sum of the income lines: {income_sum:,.0f} billion")
print(f"GDI: {y.gdi:,.0f} billion;  GDP: {y.gdp:,.0f} billion;  gap: {share(y.gdi - y.gdp, y.gdp):.2f}% of GDP")
```

In the current data, compensation is 51.6 percent of GDP in 2022, below the textbook's 53.2 percent:
the 2023 revision raised the operating surplus of businesses by about half a trillion dollars.
Depreciation, the wear and tear of capital, is about 16.5 percent of GDP.

**A note on Table 2.3 (Beyond GDP).** The textbook reports Jones and Klenow's welfare measure, which
adds life expectancy, leisure and consumption inequality to consumption per person. It shows that
Western Europe is closer to the United States than GDP suggests, and most poor countries further
away. The measure needs household-survey data on consumption inequality that are not openly
available, so we do not rebuild it here.

## Prices and inflation

Nominal GDP rises when prices rise and when production rises. These figures pull out the price part: the price level and its growth rate, inflation.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 4: The level of the GDP deflator

**Goal.** Follow the U.S. price level since 1947, as measured by the **GDP deflator**.

The GDP deflator is the price level in equation (4): nominal GDP divided by real GDP. It is an
**index**: its value in a chosen base year is set to 100. The data are quarterly, with one row per
quarter labeled by the first day of the quarter.

> **Python note.** `parse_dates=["date"]` tells pandas that the `date` column holds dates, not plain
> text. Plotly then draws a proper time axis, and we can pick rows by year.

```{python}
deflator = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig2-4.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv")
deflator.tail()
```

FRED shades the recessions in gray. The file `recessions.csv` lists the first and last month of each
recession since 1947, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER).

> **Python note.** `range(len(recessions))` gives the row numbers 0, 1, 2, …, so the `for` loop visits
> every recession once. `fig.add_vrect` draws a vertical band between two dates.

```{python}
def shade_recessions(fig):
    """Add a gray band for every NBER recession, as FRED does (Figs. 2.4 and 2.5)."""
    for i in range(len(recessions)):
        fig.add_vrect(x0=recessions.start[i], x1=recessions.end[i], fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.25, line_width=0)
    return fig
```

The World Bank publishes the GDP deflator of about 200 countries, once a year. Each country publishes
its index with its own base year, so `deflator_world.csv` has been **rebased**: every country's deflator
is divided by its 2012 value and multiplied by 100, like the U.S. series. The file also holds the
yearly inflation rate of each deflator, which Fig. 5 uses. We place each yearly value in the middle of
its year.

> **Python note.** `.astype(str)` turns numbers into text, so `deflators.year.astype(str) + "-07-01"`
> builds dates such as `"2012-07-01"`, and `pd.to_datetime` turns that text into real dates.

```{python}
deflators = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "deflator_world.csv")
deflators["date"] = pd.to_datetime(deflators.year.astype(str) + "-07-01")   # mid-year
print("Every country's deflator in 2012:", deflators[deflators.year == 2012].deflator_2012_100.dropna().unique())
deflators[deflators.country == "Japan"].tail(3)
```

The chart draws the U.S. quarterly series and, if you choose them, other countries' yearly series. When a
chosen country's prices were far lower or higher, the axis widens tenfold until every value fits.

> **Python note.** A `while` loop repeats its indented lines as long as its condition is true: here it
> multiplies the top of the axis by 10 until the largest value fits below it (and divides the bottom of
> the ratio scale by 10 until the smallest value fits above it).

```{python}
def deflator_chart(scale="linear", chosen=()):
    """Fig. 2.4: the GDP deflator (2012 = 100), U.S. quarterly since 1947, other countries yearly."""
    fig = px.line(deflator, x="date", y="gdp_deflator_2012_100", log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
                  labels={"date": "Quarter", "gdp_deflator_2012_100": "GDP deflator (index, 2012 = 100)"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), name="United States (quarterly)", showlegend=True)
    extra = deflators[deflators.country.isin(chosen)].dropna(subset=["deflator_2012_100"])
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.deflator_2012_100, name=name, line=dict(color=COLORS[name])))
    shade_recessions(fig)
    shown = pd.concat([deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100, extra.deflator_2012_100])
    low, high = 9, (170 if scale == "ratio" else 150)
    while low > shown.min():
        low = low / 10                   # widen the axis tenfold at a time until every value fits
    while high < shown.max():
        high = high * 10
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[10, 20, 40, 80, 160] if (low, high) == (9, 170) else None,
                         range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high])
    factor = deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100.iloc[-1] / deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100.iloc[0]
    fig.update_layout(title=f"The U.S. price level rose about {factor:.0f}-fold from 1947 to 2026")
    return fig
```

**What to notice.**

- Prices rose slowly until the mid-1960s, much faster in the 1970s and early 1980s, and then at a
  steadier pace, until the jump of 2021–2022.
- On the linear scale the line rises about as steeply in the 2000s as in the 1970s, because the same
  percentage increase adds more index points when prices are already high. Switch to the ratio scale:
  there the slope is the *percentage* rate of change, and the 1970s clearly stand out.
- Add Japan: its deflator *fell* from 119 in 1994 to 100 in 2013, two decades of deflation. Add Turkey on the
  ratio scale: its price level in 2025 was more than 30,000 times its 1990 level.

> **Python note.** With dates as row labels, `level["1965"]` picks the four quarters of 1965, and
> `.mean()` averages them. The formula $(\text{end}/\text{start})^{1/\text{years}} - 1$ is the average
> annual growth rate.

```{python}
level = deflator.set_index("date").gdp_deflator_2012_100
for start, end in [(1947, 1965), (1965, 1983), (1983, 2019), (2019, 2025)]:
    yearly = (level[str(end)].mean() / level[str(start)].mean()) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1
    print(f"{start}-{end}: prices rose {yearly:.1%} a year on average")
```

#### Key numbers: nominal GDP = price level × real GDP

The textbook asks how much more real GDP the United States produced in 2022 than in 1995. Real GDP in
our national accounts file is measured in chained 2017 dollars.

```{python}
nominal_ratio = nipa.loc[2022, "gdp"] / nipa.loc[1995, "gdp"]
real_ratio = nipa.loc[2022, "real_gdp"] / nipa.loc[1995, "real_gdp"]
print(f"Nominal GDP: ${nipa.loc[1995, 'gdp'] / 1000:.1f} trillion (1995), ${nipa.loc[2022, 'gdp'] / 1000:.1f} trillion (2022)")
print(f"Nominal GDP grew by a factor of {nominal_ratio:.2f}")
print(f"Real GDP grew by a factor of    {real_ratio:.2f}")
print(f"So the price level grew by      {nominal_ratio / real_ratio:.2f}")
```

Nominal GDP more than tripled, but real GDP did not quite double: the rest of the rise came from a
price level that went up by about three-quarters. (The textbook's \$7.4 trillion for 1995 is now \$7.6 trillion after
revisions.)

Taking growth rates of equation (4) gives a handy approximation (equation 7): the growth of nominal GDP is about
the growth of the price level plus the growth of real GDP.

> **Python note.** `.pct_change()` computes the change from the previous row as a fraction, for every
> row at once. The first row has no previous row, so it gets `NaN` ("not a number").

```{python}
growth = 100 * nipa[["gdp", "real_gdp"]].pct_change()
growth["prices"] = 100 * (nipa.gdp / nipa.real_gdp).pct_change()
growth["prices + real"] = growth.prices + growth.real_gdp
growth.loc[2019:].round(2)
```

In 2022, for example, nominal GDP grew 9.7 percent: prices rose 7.1 percent and real GDP 2.4 percent.
The sum, 9.6 percent, is very close. The rule is only approximate because the exact relation multiplies
growth factors: $1.097 = 1.071 \times 1.024$.

### Fig. 5: The annual inflation rate using the GDP deflator

**Goal.** Turn the price level into an **inflation rate**, the percentage change of the price level.

FRED's "Percent Change from Year Ago" compares each quarter with the same quarter one year earlier:

$$\pi_t = 100 \times \left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-4}} - 1\right)$$

where $P_t$ is the GDP deflator in quarter $t$. A second common measure compares each quarter with the
quarter before and turns the change into an annual rate: $100 \times \left[(P_t/P_{t-1})^4 - 1\right]$.

> **Python note.** `.shift(4)` moves a column down by four rows, so that each quarter sits next to the
> value from one year earlier. The first four rows get `NaN`, because there is nothing to compare them with.

```{python}
year_ago = 100 * (level / level.shift(4) - 1)
quarterly = 100 * ((level / level.shift(1)) ** 4 - 1)
rates = pd.DataFrame({"change from a year ago": year_ago, "quarterly change, annual rate": quarterly})
rates.tail()
```

The file `fig2-5.csv` holds FRED's year-ago inflation rate. Our own calculation should match it.

```{python}
inflation = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig2-5.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date")
gap = (year_ago.loc[inflation.index] - inflation.inflation_gdpdef).abs().max()
print(f"Largest difference from FRED's numbers: {gap:.4f} percentage points")
```

> **Python note.** `.dropna()` drops the rows that hold `NaN`, here the first quarters. A date knows its
> parts: `last.date.year` is its year and `last.date.quarter` its quarter (1 to 4).

Other countries can be added with their yearly GDP-deflator inflation from `deflators` (Fig. 4). The
vertical axis runs from −5 to 16 percent, and doubles at either end until every chosen value fits.

```{python}
def inflation_chart(measure="change from a year ago", chosen=()):
    """Fig. 2.5: inflation of the GDP deflator since 1947, with recession bands; other countries yearly."""
    series = rates[measure].dropna().reset_index()
    fig = px.line(series, x="date", y=measure, labels={"date": "Quarter", measure: "Inflation (percent)"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2), name="United States (quarterly)", showlegend=True)
    extra = deflators[deflators.country.isin(chosen)].dropna(subset=["inflation"])
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.inflation, name=name, line=dict(color=COLORS[name])))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    shade_recessions(fig)
    shown = pd.concat([series[measure], extra.inflation])
    low, high = -5, 16
    while low > shown.min():
        low = low * 2                    # widen the axis in steps until every value fits
    while high < shown.max():
        high = high * 2
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high])
    last = series.iloc[-1]
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Inflation, {measure}: {last[measure]:.1f}% in {last.date.year} Q{last.date.quarter}")
    return fig
```

**What to notice.**

- Inflation has two big waves: the Great Inflation of the 1970s and early 1980s, and the surge of
  2021–2022. In between, it mostly stayed between about 1 and 4 percent.
- Prices actually *fell* in 1949–1950. Inflation also came close to zero in 2009, during the Great
  Recession.
- The quarterly measure is much noisier: a single unusual quarter moves it a lot. That is why FRED's
  default for inflation compares with a year ago.
- Add Japan: its GDP deflator fell in 18 of the 20 years from 1994 to 2013. Add China: its prices fell in
  2023, 2024 and 2025. Falling prices are not only a thing of the 1930s.

yearly = year_ago.dropna()
for start, end in [("1948", "1950"), ("1950", "1952"), ("1973", "1976"), ("1979", "1982"), ("2008", "2010"),

The peaks are 8.6 percent in 1951 (the Korean War), 10.9 percent in early 1975, 10.2 percent in early
1981 and 7.8 percent in 2022; the troughs are −2.0 percent in late 1949 and 0.1 percent in mid-2009.
These match the textbook's figure, except that the 2022 peak is a little higher after the data revisions.
(Dates show the first month of each quarter.)

## Concluding remarks

- GDP is the market value of final goods and services. Value added adds up to final sales, equation (1),
  and every dollar of it is someone's income, so production, expenditure and income give the same total
  (up to a small statistical discrepancy).
- The national income identity, equation (2), splits spending. In the United States, consumption is about
  two-thirds of GDP, and since the 1970s its rise has been matched by falling government purchases and a
  trade deficit.
- Labor earns roughly two-thirds of income (equation 3), but its share has drifted down since 1970 and is
  now below 60 percent.
- Real GDP values production at common prices, and the price level links it to nominal GDP, equation (4).
  The Laspeyres and Paasche indexes are averages of the goods' growth rates with different weights,
  equation (5), and chain weighting averages the two, equation (6). Nominal growth is about inflation plus
  real growth, equation (7). Comparing countries also needs common prices, equation (8), which shrinks the
  measured gap between rich and poor countries.
- The next chapter uses real GDP per person to study long-run economic growth.

### Conceptual problems

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 1 (Basic): Who adds the value in an iPhone?** In 2009 an iPhone 3GS sold in the United States for \$500. A study for the Asian Development Bank Institute ([Xing and Detert 2010](https://www.adb.org/publications/how-iphone-widens-united-states-trade-deficit-peoples-republic-china)) breaks down its cost: parts made by firms in Japan, Korea, Germany, the United States and elsewhere cost \$172.46, and assembly in China added \$6.50, so each phone left the Chinese factory at \$178.96. To keep things simple, assume that none of the parts were made in the United States.

(a) A U.S. household buys one phone for \$500. By how much do $C$, $NX$ and U.S. GDP change, by equation (2)?

(b) Use equation (1) to find how much one phone adds to China's GDP. What share of the factory price is that?

(c) U.S. trade statistics record an import of \$178.96 from China for each phone. Measured in value added, how much of that is China's? What does this say about the U.S. trade deficit with China?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

In equation (2) the phone enters consumption at the price the household pays, and the imported part leaves again through net exports. For China, value added is what it sells minus the parts it buys.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) Consumption rises by the full price, $\Delta C = +\$500$. The phone was made abroad, so imports rise by its factory price and $\Delta NX = -\$178.96$. Investment and government purchases do not change. By equation (2),

$$\Delta Y = \Delta C + \Delta NX = 500 - 178.96 = \$321.04.$$

The \$321.04 is U.S. value added: the design, software and brand of the U.S. company, plus the shipping, wholesale, retail and advertising that bring the phone to the buyer.

(b) China's factory sells the phone for \$178.96 and buys parts worth \$172.46, so by equation (1) its value added is

$$VA_{\text{China}} = 178.96 - 172.46 = \$6.50, \qquad \frac{6.50}{178.96} = 3.6\%\text{ of the factory price}.$$

(c) Only \$6.50 of the \$178.96 is Chinese value added. The other \$172.46 is value added in Japan, Korea, Germany and the other countries that made the parts, which reaches the United States through China. A trade balance in gross values assigns the whole phone to the last country in the chain, so it overstates the U.S. deficit with China and understates the deficits with the countries that make the parts. The total U.S. trade deficit is the same either way; only its split by country changes. (In fact, \$10.75 of the parts came from U.S. firms. If they were made in the United States, U.S. exports rise by \$10.75, and the phone adds $500 - 178.96 + 10.75 = \$331.79$ to U.S. GDP.)

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 2 (Intermediate): Ireland's 26 percent year.** In July 2016, Ireland's Central Statistics Office (CSO) reported that real GDP had grown by 26 percent in 2015, while employment grew by only 2.3 percent. In its [explanation](https://www.cso.ie/en/media/csoie/methods/nationalincomeandexpenditureannualresults/NIE_2016_FAQS.pdf), the CSO says that multinational firms moved whole balance sheets into Ireland, mostly intellectual property such as patents, which added €300 billion to Ireland's capital stock. Its numbers, in billions of euros at current prices:

| | 2014 | 2015 |
|---|---|---|
| GDP | 194.5 | 262.0 |
| Net exports of goods and services | 35 | 80 |
| GNI: GDP minus the net income paid abroad | 165.9 | 207.2 |
| Depreciation of the relocated intellectual property | 0.8 | 25.0 |
| GNI\* ("modified GNI"): GNI minus that depreciation and other multinational effects | 154.5 | 172.9 |
| Government gross debt | 203.3 | 201.4 |

(a) Compute the growth of nominal GDP, GNI and GNI\* from 2014 to 2015.

(b) Write equation (2) in changes. What fraction of the rise in GDP came from net exports?

(c) The depreciation of relocated patents rose from €0.8 billion to €25.0 billion. Why does it count in GDP? And who receives most of the extra profit?

(d) Government debt as a share of GDP fell from 104.5 to 76.9 percent. Compute the debt ratio with GNI\* instead. Which ratio tells you more about the burden of the debt on Irish taxpayers?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

A growth rate is new/old − 1. For (b), take the change of each side of equation (2). For (c), go back to the income split of value added in Step 2 of the Model overview, and ask who owns the multinationals. For (d), divide the same debt by a different measure of income.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) Nominal GDP grew $262.0/194.5 - 1 = 34.7$ percent, GNI $207.2/165.9 - 1 = 24.9$ percent, and GNI\* $172.9/154.5 - 1 = 11.9$ percent. The more of the multinationals' activity a measure removes, the slower it grows.

(b) In changes, $\Delta Y = \Delta C + \Delta I + \Delta G + \Delta NX$. GDP rose by $262.0 - 194.5 = 67.5$ billion euros, and net exports by $80 - 35 = 45$ billion, so net exports account for $45/67.5 = 2/3$ of the rise. The reason, in the CSO's account: products made abroad under contract for firms whose patents now sit in Ireland are counted as Irish exports, and the royalties that Irish subsidiaries used to pay abroad for the patents (imports of services) disappeared. Our World Bank data in Fig. 1 show the same jump: Ireland's net exports went from 19.0 percent of GDP in 2014 to 29.7 percent in 2015.

(c) GDP is *gross*: Step 2 of the Model overview splits it into compensation, taxes on production, the net operating surplus **and depreciation**. The wear and tear of patents located in Ireland is therefore part of Irish value added, even though it pays no one's income in Ireland. The rest of the extra value added is profit (operating surplus) of firms owned abroad, and it is paid to their foreign owners: the gap between GDP and GNI widened from $194.5 - 165.9 = 28.6$ to $262.0 - 207.2 = 54.8$ billion euros. Employment grew only 2.3 percent, so little of the new value added was labor income. It shows in the labor share of Fig. 3: in our Penn World Table data, Ireland's labor share fell from 0.451 in 2014 to 0.339 in 2015.

(d) With GNI\* in the denominator, the debt ratio was

$$\frac{203.3}{154.5} = 131.6\% \text{ in 2014}, \qquad \frac{201.4}{172.9} = 116.5\% \text{ in 2015}.$$

The debt itself barely changed (it fell by 1.9 billion euros). Its ratio to GDP dropped by 27.6 points only because GDP jumped, and much of that jump is not income of Irish residents: it is the depreciation of relocated patents and profits paid to foreign owners. GNI\* measures the income of Irish residents better, so it gives a fairer picture of the burden; the CSO itself presents GNI\* as a measure for budget and fiscal analysis.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 3 (Challenge): Why chained components do not add up.** A hypothetical island produces only fish, which households eat (consumption $C$), and boats, which fishers buy (investment $I$):

| | Year 1 | Year 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Price of fish (dollars) | 2 | 3 |
| Quantity of fish | 100 | 110 |
| Price of boats (dollars) | 50 | 40 |
| Quantity of boats | 4 | 6 |

The island's statistics office publishes chained real values, as the BEA does, with year 2 as the benchmark year. The BEA warns that such chained components need not add up to chained GDP ([NIPA Handbook, Chapter 4](https://www.bea.gov/resources/methodologies/nipa-handbook/pdf/chapter-04.pdf)).

(a) Compute nominal GDP in both years, the Laspeyres and Paasche growth rates of real GDP, and the chain-weighted growth rate, equation (6).

(b) Compute chained real GDP in year 1, and chained real $C$ and $I$ in year 1.

(c) Show that chained $C$ plus chained $I$ differs from chained GDP in year 1. Then prove, for any number of goods, that the sum of the chained one-good components in year 1 equals $\sum_i p_{i,2}\,q_{i,1}$, and that it is larger than chained GDP whenever $g^L > g^P$.

(d) A journalist computes the investment share of year 1 as chained investment divided by chained GDP. What does she find, what is the right number, and why?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

A component with a single good grows exactly as fast as its quantity under every index, so its chained value in year 1 is its year-2 value divided by its quantity growth factor. For the proof, compare your result with the denominator of the Paasche fraction in Step 1 of the real-GDP block.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) Nominal GDP is $2 \times 100 + 50 \times 4 = 400$ in year 1 and $3 \times 110 + 40 \times 6 = 570$ in year 2. At year-1 prices, year 2 is worth $2 \times 110 + 50 \times 6 = 520$; at year-2 prices, year 1 is worth $3 \times 100 + 40 \times 4 = 460$. So

$$1 + g^L = \frac{520}{400} = 1.300, \qquad 1 + g^P = \frac{570}{460} = 1.2391, \qquad g^{\text{chain}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(30.0\% + 23.9\%) = 27.0\%.$$

(b) Chained GDP equals nominal GDP in the benchmark year, 570, so in year 1 it is $570/1.26957 = 448.97$. Fish grew 10 percent and boats 50 percent, so chained $C$ in year 1 is $330/1.10 = 300$ and chained $I$ is $240/1.50 = 160$.

(c) $300 + 160 = 460$, which is 11.03 more than chained GDP (448.97). In general, a one-good component $i$ has the chained value

$$X_{i,1} = \frac{p_{i,2}\,q_{i,2}}{q_{i,2}/q_{i,1}} = p_{i,2}\,q_{i,1} \qquad\text{so}\qquad \sum_i X_{i,1} = \sum_i p_{i,2}\,q_{i,1} = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,2}\,q_{i,2}}{1 + g^P},$$

where the last step is the definition of the Paasche index in Step 1. Chained GDP is instead $X_1 = \sum_i p_{i,2}\,q_{i,2}\,/\,(1 + g^{\text{chain}})$. By equation (6), $g^{\text{chain}} - g^P = \tfrac{1}{2}(g^L - g^P)$, so when $g^L > g^P$ the chain-weighted growth rate is larger than the Paasche rate, its denominator is larger, and chained GDP is smaller than the sum of the components. In the benchmark year the two agree, so the gap appears only away from it; the BEA shows it as a "residual" line in its chained-dollar tables.

(d) She finds $160/448.97 = 35.6$ percent. The right share uses nominal values, which do add up: $200/400 = 50.0$ percent in year 1 (and $240/570 = 42.1$ percent in year 2). Chained year-1 values use year-2 relative prices, and boats became relatively cheaper, so chained values understate the weight of boats in year 1. That is why the Model overview says: shares from nominal values, growth rates from chained values.

</details>

**Problem 4 (Basic): Has labor's share fallen across the G7?** Fig. 3 shows labor's share of U.S. income drifting down since 1970. Is that true of all rich countries? Use the labor shares of the [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) in `labor_share_world.csv`, and the G7 flag of the [World Bank country classifications](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups) in `countries.csv`. Compare 1990 and 2019 (the last year before the pandemic) for the seven G7 countries. In how many did the labor share fall? Which country had the largest fall, and which the largest rise? Is "two-thirds" a good description of the G7 in 2019?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Keep the rows of the G7 countries (`countries.csv` has a True/False column `g7`) and the two years, with `.isin(...)`. Then `.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="labor_share")` puts the two years side by side, one row per country.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

We keep the G7 rows for 1990 and 2019, put the two years side by side, and subtract.

```python
pwt_shares = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "labor_share_world.csv")
groups = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
g7_names = groups[groups.g7].country
g7 = pwt_shares[pwt_shares.country.isin(g7_names) & pwt_shares.year.isin([1990, 2019])]
table = g7.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="labor_share")
table["change"] = table[2019] - table[1990]
print(table.sort_values("change").round(3))
print("G7 countries where the share fell:", (table.change < 0).sum())
print(f"G7 average in 2019: {table[2019].mean():.3f}")
```

The share fell in four of the seven countries: Canada (−0.052, the largest fall), Italy (−0.038), the United States (−0.023) and France (−0.001, hardly a change). It rose in Germany (+0.005), Japan (+0.010) and the United Kingdom (+0.017, the largest rise). So the decline is not universal. In 2019 the shares ranged from 0.537 in Italy to 0.659 in Canada, with a G7 average of 0.610: closer to 60 percent than to two-thirds. Remember that the Penn World Table measures the U.S. share about 0.03 below Fig. 3; in Fig. 3's own measure, the U.S. share fell from 0.653 to 0.620 over the same years.

**Problem 5 (Intermediate): Prices or production?** Equation (7) splits the growth of nominal GDP into inflation and real growth. Use the BEA's national accounts in `nipa_annual.csv`: nominal GDP (`gdp`, [`GDPA`](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA)) and real GDP in chained 2017 dollars (`real_gdp`, [`GDPCA`](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPCA)), both via FRED.

(a) Over the Great Depression, from 1929 to 1933, by what percentage did nominal GDP, real GDP and the price level (the deflator, nominal over real GDP) change?

(b) In which years did nominal GDP grow while real GDP fell? What kind of years are they?

(c) Find the three years in which the rule of thumb of equation (7) misses nominal growth by the most. What do they have in common?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Build a table with nominal GDP, real GDP and their ratio, the deflator of equation (4). `.pct_change()` gives every year's growth, as in the Key numbers of Fig. 4. For (b), join two conditions with `&`. For (c), the miss is nominal growth minus the sum of inflation and real growth.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

We compute the deflator, the change over 1929–1933, every year's growth rates, and the miss of the rule of thumb.

```python
accounts = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "nipa_annual.csv").set_index("year")
levels = pd.DataFrame({"nominal": accounts.gdp, "real": accounts.real_gdp})
levels["prices"] = levels.nominal / levels.real            # the GDP deflator, equation (4)
print("Percent change, 1929-1933:")
print((100 * (levels.loc[1933] / levels.loc[1929] - 1)).round(1))
growth_rates = 100 * levels.pct_change()
growth_rates["miss"] = growth_rates.nominal - (growth_rates.prices + growth_rates.real)
print(growth_rates[(growth_rates.nominal > 0) & (growth_rates.real < 0)].round(2) + 0.0)   # + 0.0: no -0.00
print(growth_rates.miss.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).round(2))
```

(a) From 1929 to 1933, nominal GDP fell 45.3 percent, real GDP 26.3 percent and the price level 25.8 percent. The exact split multiplies growth factors: $(1 - 0.263)(1 - 0.258) = 0.547 \approx 1 - 0.453$. About half of the collapse in spending was falling prices, and half falling production.

(b) Nominal GDP grew while real GDP fell in nine years: 1945, 1947, 1954, 1958, 1974, 1975, 1980, 1982 and 1991. Most are recession years (1954, 1958, 1974–1975, 1980, 1982, 1991), and 1945 and 1947 are the end of World War II, when war production was wound down. In all of them prices rose faster than production fell. The clearest cases are the stagflation years 1974, 1975 and 1980, with inflation of about 9 percent and falling output: measured in dollars, the economy grew while it produced less.

(c) The misses are largest in 1932, by 1.51 points, and in 1942 and 1946, by 1.50 points each. The miss is the cross term $\pi\,g_{\text{real}}$, the product of the two rates, so it is large only when inflation and real growth are both large. In 1932 prices fell 11.7 percent and output 12.9 percent; in 1942, the war boom, output rose 18.9 percent and prices 7.9 percent; in 1946, after the war, output fell 11.6 percent while prices rose 12.9 percent.

</details>

**Problem 6 (Challenge): Are rich countries more expensive?** The Model overview argues that poor countries have low price levels, so that comparisons at exchange rates exaggerate the income gaps between countries. Test this with `ppp_world.csv`, a file prepared for this problem from the World Bank's World Development Indicators: GDP at market exchange rates in billions of current dollars (`gdp_usd_bn`, [`NY.GDP.MKTP.CD`](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD)), GDP at purchasing power parity in billions of international dollars (`gdp_ppp_bn`, [`NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.CD`](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.CD)) and population in millions (`population_m`, [`SP.POP.TOTL`](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL)), for about 200 economies from 1990 to 2025. An international dollar buys as much as a U.S. dollar buys in the United States.

(a) Solve equation (8) for the relative price level. Compute it, and GDP per person at PPP, for every economy in 2024 (leave out the "Euro area" aggregate).

(b) Compute the correlation between the log price level and log GDP per person, and the slope of a straight line through them. What does the slope mean?

(c) Rank the economies by GDP in 2024, once at exchange rates and once at PPP. Which economy is the largest by each measure? Among the ten largest at PPP, which climb the most places, and which economies drop out of the top ten?

(d) Find the exceptions: the economies with GDP per person above \$60,000 but a price level below 0.55, and those with GDP per person below \$10,000 but a price level above 0.75. What do the members of each group have in common?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

In equation (8), dollar GDP is on one side and GDP at common prices on the other, so their ratio is the relative price level. Take logs with `np.log`. `np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]` is the correlation, and `np.polyfit(x, y, 1)` returns the slope first, as in Fig. 3. For (c), `.rank(ascending=False)` gives the largest economy rank 1. For (d), join two conditions with `&`.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Equation (8) says that GDP at common prices is dollar GDP divided by the relative price level, so the relative price level is dollar GDP divided by GDP at common prices: $\text{price level}_i/\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}} = \text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_i \,/\, \text{real GDP}^{\text{common prices}}_i$. For the United States the two GDPs are equal, so its price level is 1.

```python
ppp_data = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "ppp_world.csv")
y2024 = ppp_data[(ppp_data.year == 2024) & (ppp_data.country != "Euro area")].copy()
y2024["price_level"] = y2024.gdp_usd_bn / y2024.gdp_ppp_bn          # equation (8), solved
y2024["income"] = 1000 * y2024.gdp_ppp_bn / y2024.population_m      # dollars per person, PPP
log_income, log_price = np.log(y2024.income), np.log(y2024.price_level)
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(log_income, log_price, 1)
print(f"{len(y2024)} economies; correlation {np.corrcoef(log_income, log_price)[0, 1]:.2f}; slope {slope:.3f}")
y2024["rank_usd"] = y2024.gdp_usd_bn.rank(ascending=False)              # 1 = largest
y2024["rank_ppp"] = y2024.gdp_ppp_bn.rank(ascending=False)
print(y2024.nsmallest(10, "rank_ppp")[["country", "rank_usd", "rank_ppp", "price_level"]].round(2))
print(y2024[(y2024.rank_usd <= 10) & (y2024.rank_ppp > 10)][["country", "rank_usd", "rank_ppp"]])
print(y2024[(y2024.income > 60000) & (y2024.price_level < 0.55)][["country", "income", "price_level"]].round(2))
print(y2024[(y2024.income < 10000) & (y2024.price_level > 0.75)][["country", "income", "price_level"]].round(2))
```

(b) Across 195 economies, the correlation of the logs is 0.53 and the slope is 0.196: the slope of a line in logs is an elasticity, so 10 percent more GDP per person goes with a price level about 1.9 percent higher ($1.1^{0.196} = 1.019$), and a country twice as rich is about $2^{0.196} = 1.15$ times as expensive. The fact holds, though with a lot of spread around the line.

(c) At exchange rates the United States is the largest economy, followed by China, Germany, Japan and India. At PPP China is the largest, followed by the United States, India, Russia and Japan: China's price level is only 0.49 of the U.S. level, so its GDP at common prices passes U.S. GDP. Among the ten largest at PPP, Indonesia climbs the most (from 16th to 8th), then Russia (10th to 4th) and Brazil (11th to 7th), all with low price levels (0.30 to 0.46 of the U.S. level). Italy (8th) and Canada (9th) drop out of the top ten (to 12th and 16th). Moving to common prices lifts the poorer economies and lowers the richer ones, as equation (8) and part (b) predict.

(d) The rich but cheap economies are Bahrain, Brunei, Guyana and Saudi Arabia. All four live on oil and gas: in 2021 the World Bank put their oil and gas rents at between 17 and 25 percent of GDP ([oil rents](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PETR.RT.ZS), [natural gas rents](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.NGAS.RT.ZS)). Their GDP per person is high because of that revenue rather than because of high wages across the whole economy, so labor-intensive services stay cheap. The poor but expensive ones are the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu: small, remote island economies in the Pacific. A likely reason is that much of what they consume has to be shipped in over long distances, a hypothesis you could test with the World Bank's data on [imports of goods and services](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS).

</details>

### Modeling problems

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 7 (Basic): A target for nominal GDP.** Some economists have proposed that central banks target the growth of nominal GDP instead of inflation; [Hetzel (2015)](https://www.richmondfed.org/publications/research/economic_brief/2015/eb_15-04), at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, reviews the idea and argues that a strict target could destabilize the economy. Suppose a central bank keeps nominal GDP growing at 4 percent a year.

(a) If real GDP grows 2 percent, what inflation does the target imply?

(b) A recession cuts real growth to −2 percent. What inflation does the same target imply now? And if a technology boom raises real growth to 3.5 percent?

(c) Compare with a central bank that keeps inflation at 2 percent whatever happens: what is nominal GDP growth in the three cases?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Equation (7) gives the rule of thumb. For the exact answer, solve $1 + g_{\text{nominal}} = (1+\pi)(1+g_{\text{real}})$ for $\pi$. For (b), move only the real-growth slider.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def nominal_target(target=4.0, real_growth=2.0):
    """Inflation implied by a nominal-GDP growth target: exact, and by the rule of thumb of equation (7)."""
    inflation = round(100 * ((1 + target / 100) / (1 + real_growth / 100) - 1), 2) + 0.0
    rule = round(target - real_growth, 2) + 0.0
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=["Nominal GDP (target)", "Real GDP", "Inflation, exact", "Inflation, equation (7)"],
                           y=[target, real_growth, inflation, rule], marker_color=[BLUE, GREEN, TEAL, GRAY],
                           texttemplate="%{y:+.2f}%"))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"A {target:.1f}% target with {real_growth:+.1f}% real growth implies {inflation:.2f}% inflation",
                      yaxis=dict(title="Growth rate (percent a year)", range=[-8, 14]))
    return fig


interact(nominal_target,
         target=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=0.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="nominal GDP target (%)", style=WIDE),
         real_growth=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=-4.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="real GDP growth (%)", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** A calculator built on equation (7) of the Model overview, adapted from the discussion of nominal GDP, real GDP and inflation in Chapter 2 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Solving the exact relation for inflation gives $\pi = (1 + g_{\text{nominal}})/(1 + g_{\text{real}}) - 1$, and equation (7) gives $\pi \approx g_{\text{nominal}} - g_{\text{real}}$.

(a) With real growth of 2 percent: $\pi = 1.04/1.02 - 1 = 1.96$ percent, close to the rule of thumb's 2 percent.

(b) With −2 percent: $\pi = 1.04/0.98 - 1 = 6.12$ percent (rule of thumb 6 percent). With 3.5 percent: $\pi = 1.04/1.035 - 1 = 0.48$ percent (rule of thumb 0.5). With the target met, each point less real growth means about one point more inflation: the target splits a slowdown between output and prices, and lets inflation rise in a recession.

(c) With inflation held at 2 percent, nominal GDP grows $1.02 \times (1 + g_{\text{real}}) - 1$: 4.04 percent with 2 percent real growth, −0.04 percent with −2 percent, and 5.57 percent with 3.5 percent. Under an inflation target, nominal GDP growth swings with real growth; under a nominal-GDP target, inflation does. When output falls, a nominal-GDP target accepts higher inflation. Whether that is wise depends on what caused the fall, and is a question for the models of later chapters; the accounting only tells you how the burden is split.

```python
for g_real in [2.0, -2.0, 3.5]:
    pi = 100 * (1.04 / (1 + g_real / 100) - 1)
    nominal = 100 * (1.02 * (1 + g_real / 100) - 1)
    print(f"real growth {g_real:+.1f}%: inflation under the target {pi:.2f}%, "
          f"nominal growth under 2% inflation {nominal:.2f}%")
```

</details>

**Problem 8 (Intermediate): A weaker yuan and the IMF's measure of size.** The IMF gives each member a quota, which determines its voting power and its access to IMF resources ([IMF factsheet](https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2022/IMF-Quotas)). The quota formula agreed in 2008 measures each economy's size with a blend of GDP: 60 percent at market exchange rates and 40 percent at PPP ([IMF 2008, Reform of Quota and Voice](https://www.imf.org/external/np/pp/eng/2008/032108.pdf)). The calculator applies this blend to China and the United States, starting from the textbook's 2019 numbers of Check 7: China's GDP of 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar, Chinese prices at 68.4 percent of U.S. prices, and U.S. GDP of \$20.6 trillion, which stays fixed. (The IMF itself works with each country's share of world GDP.)

(a) From 2019 to 2024 the yuan weakened from 6.91 to 7.20 per dollar ([FRED `AEXCHUS`](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/AEXCHUS)). With China's yuan prices and output unchanged, how do the three measures change?

(b) Go back to 6.91. By how much would China's real output have to grow, with prices unchanged, for the blend to reach 100 percent of U.S. GDP? Find it with the sliders, then solve for it.

(c) Now let China's yuan prices rise 10 percent, with the exchange rate at 6.91 and output unchanged. What happens to each measure? Which weighting of the blend would China prefer, and why?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Dollar GDP is yuan GDP divided by $e$. At common prices the exchange rate cancels, because China's price level in dollars moves with $1/e$ too (Step 4 of the PPP block). For (b), notice that all three measures are proportional to China's output.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def china_size(e=6.91, prices=0, output=0):
    """China's GDP in percent of U.S. GDP: at the exchange rate, at common prices (equation 8) and a 60/40 blend."""
    yuan_gdp = 95.1 * (1 + prices / 100) * (1 + output / 100)       # trillions of yuan (2019: 95.1)
    relative_price = 0.684 * (6.91 / e) * (1 + prices / 100)        # China's price level / U.S. price level
    dollars = to_dollars(yuan_gdp, e)
    common = at_common_prices(dollars, relative_price)
    sizes = [100 * dollars / 20.6, 100 * common / 20.6, 100 * (0.6 * dollars + 0.4 * common) / 20.6]
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=["At the exchange rate", "At common prices (PPP)", "IMF-style blend (60/40)"],
                           y=sizes, marker_color=[TEAL, GREEN, BLUE], texttemplate="%{y:.1f}"))
    fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dash", line_color="black")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{e:.2f} yuan per dollar; Chinese prices at {100 * relative_price:.1f}% of U.S. prices",
                      yaxis=dict(title="China's GDP (U.S. GDP = 100)", range=[0, 160]))
    return fig


interact(china_size,
         e=FloatSlider(value=6.91, min=6.0, max=8.0, step=0.01, description="yuan per dollar e", style=WIDE),
         prices=IntSlider(value=0, min=0, max=30, step=1, description="rise in yuan prices (%)", style=WIDE),
         output=IntSlider(value=0, min=0, max=40, step=1, description="rise in real output (%)", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** A calculator built on equation (8) and the conversion functions of the Model overview, adapted from the China–U.S. comparison in Chapter 2 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612); it starts from the textbook's 2019 numbers.

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

At the start, China's GDP is 66.8 percent of U.S. GDP at the exchange rate, 97.7 percent at common prices, and $0.6 \times 66.8 + 0.4 \times 97.7 = 79.2$ percent in the blend.

(a) At 7.20 yuan per dollar, dollar GDP falls by $6.91/7.20 - 1 = -4.0$ percent, to 64.1 percent of U.S. GDP. GDP at common prices does not move (97.7), because China's goods are cheaper in dollars by the same 4 percent: its relative price level falls from 68.4 to 65.6 percent. The blend falls to 77.5 percent, by 60 percent of the exchange-rate effect. A weaker currency makes a country look smaller in dollars without changing what it produces.

(b) All three measures are proportional to China's output, so the blend reaches 100 percent when $(1 + g) \times 0.7916 = 1$, that is $g = 1/0.7916 - 1 = 26.3$ percent. With the slider, 26 percent gives 99.7 and 27 percent gives 100.5.

(c) Yuan prices 10 percent higher raise dollar GDP by 10 percent, to 73.5 percent of U.S. GDP, and China's relative price level from 68.4 to 75.2 percent. GDP at common prices is unchanged at 97.7, since only prices moved. The blend rises to 83.2 percent. China's price level is low, so it looks much larger at PPP than at the exchange rate; the more weight the formula puts on PPP GDP, the larger China's measured size and its quota. With a weight of 100 percent on PPP, the blend would be 97.7 instead of 79.2.

```python
for e_rate, price_rise, output_rise in [(6.91, 0, 0), (7.20, 0, 0), (6.91, 0, 26), (6.91, 0, 27), (6.91, 10, 0)]:
    bars = china_size(e_rate, price_rise, output_rise).data[0].y
    print(f"e = {e_rate}, prices +{price_rise}%, output +{output_rise}%: "
          f"{bars[0]:.1f}, {bars[1]:.1f}, {bars[2]:.1f} percent of U.S. GDP")
```

**Problem 9 (Challenge): How fast does a base year go out of date?** Until 1996 the BEA valued real GDP at the prices of a fixed base year, which it updated about every five years; then it switched to chain weighting. In its [NIPA Handbook](https://www.bea.gov/resources/methodologies/nipa-handbook/pdf/chapter-04.pdf), the BEA explains that fixed weights tend to understate growth before the base year and overstate it after. The calculator follows a hypothetical economy with two goods. In the base year, services and computers both cost \$1, and the economy buys 98 units of services and 2 computers. Every year, services become 3 percent more expensive and their quantity grows 2 percent; the sliders set the yearly change of the price and the quantity of computers. The bars show real GDP growth from one year to the next, measured at base-year prices and with the indexes of equations (5) and (6).

(a) With computer prices falling 20 percent a year and their quantity growing 30 percent, by how much do base-year prices overstate growth from the base year to the next, and 5, 10 and 20 years later?

(b) The statistical office decides to update its base year as soon as the overstatement exceeds 1 percentage point. How often must it update?

(c) Set the yearly change of computer prices to 0, then to +3 and +5 percent (10 years after the base year). What happens to the gap, and why?

(d) Use the Laspeyres form of equation (5) to explain why growth at base-year prices drifts toward the growth rate of computers, while chain-weighted growth stays near 2.5 percent.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Move the first slider and read the gap in the title. For (d), growth at base-year prices is a weighted average of the goods' growth rates, with weights $p_{i,b}\,q_{i,t}/\sum_k p_{k,b}\,q_{k,t}$; compare how the weight of computers changes each year at base-year prices and at current prices.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def base_year_bias(years=10, computer_price=-20, computer_growth=30):
    """Real growth in one year, at base-year prices and with chain weighting (equations 5 and 6)."""
    p_base = pd.Series({"services": 1.0, "computers": 1.0})
    q_base = pd.Series({"services": 98.0, "computers": 2.0})          # computers: 2% of base-year spending
    p_step = pd.Series({"services": 1.03, "computers": 1 + computer_price / 100})
    q_step = pd.Series({"services": 1.02, "computers": 1 + computer_growth / 100})
    p_now, q_now = p_base * p_step ** years, q_base * q_step ** years
    p_next, q_next = p_now * p_step, q_now * q_step
    g_fixed = gdp_value(p_base, q_next) / gdp_value(p_base, q_now) - 1
    g_laspeyres = gdp_value(p_now, q_next) / gdp_value(p_now, q_now) - 1
    g_paasche = gdp_value(p_next, q_next) / gdp_value(p_next, q_now) - 1
    g_chain = chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche)
    gap = round(100 * (g_fixed - g_chain), 2) + 0.0
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=["Base-year prices", "Laspeyres", "Paasche", "Chain-weighted"],
                           y=[100 * g_fixed, 100 * g_laspeyres, 100 * g_paasche, 100 * g_chain],
                           marker_color=[GRAY, TEAL, GREEN, BLUE], texttemplate="%{y:.2f}%"))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Year {years} to {years + 1}: base-year prices give {100 * g_fixed:.2f}%, "
                            f"chained {100 * g_chain:.2f}% (gap {gap:+.2f} points)",
                      yaxis=dict(title="Growth of real GDP (percent)", range=[0, 45]))
    return fig


interact(base_year_bias,
         years=IntSlider(value=10, min=0, max=30, step=1, description="years since the base year", style=WIDE),
         computer_price=IntSlider(value=-20, min=-30, max=5, step=1, description="computer prices (% a year)", style=WIDE),
         computer_growth=IntSlider(value=30, min=0, max=40, step=5, description="computers bought (% a year)", style=WIDE));
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) The gap between growth at base-year prices and chain-weighted growth is 0.06 points from the base year to the next, 1.32 points five years later, 4.80 points ten years later (7.25 against 2.45 percent) and 19.84 points twenty years later. Growth at base-year prices keeps rising, while chain-weighted growth stays near 2.4–2.5 percent.

(b) The gap is 0.95 points four years after the base year and 1.32 points five years after it, so the office must update about every five years, which is roughly what the BEA used to do. Chain weighting removes the need: it updates the prices every year.

(c) Ten years after the base year, the gap is 4.80 points when computer prices fall 20 percent a year, 1.20 points when they stay constant, 0.00 when they rise 3 percent, like services, and −0.92 points when they rise 5 percent. The gap comes from **changes in relative prices**. When all prices rise at the same rate, base-year and current prices give the same weights ("When do the two agree?" in the real-GDP block). When computers become relatively cheaper, base-year prices overvalue them, and because they are also the fast-growing good, growth is overstated. When they become relatively dearer, base-year prices undervalue them, and growth is understated.

(d) Growth at base-year prices is $g^{\text{base}}_t = \sum_i w_{i,t}\,g_i$ with $w_{i,t} = p_{i,b}\,q_{i,t}/\sum_k p_{k,b}\,q_{k,t}$. At fixed prices, the weight of each good moves only with its quantity, so the ratio of the computers' weight to the services' weight grows by the factor $1.30/1.02 = 1.27$ every year. After enough years computers carry almost all the weight, and $g^{\text{base}}$ approaches their 30 percent growth. The chain-weighted index uses current spending shares, and computer spending grows by the factor $0.80 \times 1.30 = 1.04$ a year, against $1.03 \times 1.02 = 1.0506$ for services, so the computers' share of spending drifts down slowly, from 2.0 to 1.8 percent after ten years. Chain-weighted growth therefore stays close to the share-weighted average $0.98 \times 2\% + 0.02 \times 30\% = 2.56$ percent, the Laspeyres rate of the base year, and falls a little as the computers' share shrinks: it is 2.50 percent from the base year to the next and 2.45 percent ten years later.

for years in [0, 4, 5, 10, 20]:
    print(years, base_year_bias(years).layout.title.text)
for computer_price in [-20, 0, 3, 5]:
    print(computer_price, base_year_bias(10, computer_price).layout.title.text)
